\begin{abstract}
Formal mathematics projects increasingly use AI agents for drafting,
review, theorem search, and manuscript preparation.  Ungated agent output,
however, can create theorem-looking but content-poor edits, stale source
references, duplicated submission routes, and premature paper promotion.  We
report an auditable theory-to-paper pipeline used around a BEDC source
workspace with bounded Lean/source-interface evidence and an automath publication workspace.  The
pipeline separates source development, intake packets, active paper
directories, AI review loops, deterministic gates, and human promotion
decisions.  Its central rule is that AI output is advisory: load-bearing
mathematical and submission claims must be tied, at the appropriate evidence
level, to source paths, command logs, deterministic checks, and human-approved
promotion.  Under an explicit accepted record-gate-soundness row or hypothesis, the core
reviewer-facing result is the conditional RGS finite-record master presentation interface: every
load-bearing presentation claim factors through the finite architecture axes,
record-gate predicate, accepted certificate set, bad-subrecord report, and
negative-boundary fields.  The six-role factorization, finite-record publication-safety,
weak-interface maximality, finite-script projection-contract, and case-row
theorems are support coordinates for that master interface.  They construct the finite publication certificates checked by the
package verifier from recorded gate-passage entries and explicitly submitted
review surfaces; every publication-safety conclusion is therefore conditional on
that accepted RGS row or hypothesis and is deliberately certificate-level and
finite-record only.  The theorem is not an
implementation-soundness theorem, a formal-verification theorem, an
artifact-semantic theorem, or a venue-acceptance theorem: it proves neither Lean
builds, daemon behaviour, artifact semantics, nor venue acceptance.  The current
package then proves schema-relative, row-frozen finite-record certificate exactness
for its six-row, local path-verified and ledger-relative instantiation only, while rejecting stronger readings
such as external gate implementation soundness, proof-assistant correctness,
artifact semantic validity, current execution of every gate, or venue acceptance.
Four case
studies illustrate the gates at the path-verified historical-snapshot level: intake
isolation, overlap/submitted blocking, fake-extension rejection, and
artifact-limitation disclosure.
The scoped boundary normal form isolates the five presentation-package weak
points---record-gate soundness, imported source-interface evidence, finite
witness rows, primary-claim inventories, and theorem inventories---and proves that
each supports only its bounded finite-record reading unless a fresh finite upgrade
coordinate is supplied.  The support rows are local/path-verified support rows,
not clean-machine reproducibility claims.  In particular, any end-to-end workflow-correctness
reading decomposes into separate finite budgets for gate implementation audits,
fresh formal/source checks, artifact semantics, and submitted-support records; the
present package intentionally supplies the finite-record certificate level rather
than those stronger budgets.  The terminal weak-interface maximality theorem
classifies these boundaries as a finite skeleton: each stronger reading has a
unique missing upgrade coordinate and an inclusion-minimal bad subrecord.
\end{abstract}

\section{Problem and contribution}

AI assistance is useful in a formal-mathematics project only if the project can
distinguish proposal from evidence.  A generated theorem statement, a legal
piece of code, a mechanical expansion, or a lower score in a review rubric does
not by itself constitute mathematical discovery.  The practical publication
failure modes are equally structural: a route may overlap a submitted sibling,
an artifact status file may drift from generated counts, or an intake note may
accidentally become a daemon-visible manuscript.

This source is the technical supplement for the presentation-only contribution
\emph{Auditable Theory-to-Paper Pipelines for AI-Assisted Formal Mathematics},
whose single primary article source is the compact file
\path{submission_abstract.tex}.
This file is subordinate technical support, not a competing submission title
and not the object that should be read as the CICM presentation article.
The final source-level packaging convention used throughout both sources is the
following.  The primary CICM presentation-only article is
\path{submission_abstract.tex}.  The present file, \path{main.tex}, is the
submitted technical supplement that records definitions, theorem proofs, and
case-evidence tables for the compact claim.  The non-TeX support records are the
submitted source/support-package surfaces for the finite-record coordinates named
in this supplement; absent a separate archive or upload-receipt coordinate, they
are not additionally claimed to be public archive objects or externally
byte-identical uploads.  The non-TeX
paths \path{theorem_inventory.json},
\path{theorem_inventory.md}, \path{source_interface_record.json},
\path{review_bundle/}, command logs, digest records, and script-generated
inventory files are reviewer-local support surfaces: they are used here only as
finite/path-verified support coordinates, not as ordinary article claims, not as
public archive locators, and not as clean-machine reproducibility assertions.
No venue-upload receipt, DOI-bearing replacement, external supplement
availability, final archive-equivalent byte-equality locator, implementation
soundness, proof-assistant correctness, dynamic artifact validation, or venue
acceptance is claimed unless a later theorem explicitly adds the corresponding
finite upgrade coordinate.  Later references to local inventories, bundles,
digests, or logs are shorthand for this support-boundary convention.  This file
records a compact workflow pattern for avoiding these failures: an auditable
theory-to-paper pipeline in which AI agents propose, review, and triage, while
deterministic gates decide what may be treated as load-bearing evidence.  The
pattern is instantiated in local BEDC and automath workspaces.

\paragraph{Compact theorem dependency map.}
The reusable mathematical spine is the finite-record calculus, compressed for the
presentation route into five nodes: the six-role interface, record-gate soundness,
finite-record exactness, no-free-upgrade, and the four methodological case rows.
The corresponding primary-route consequence is
Corollary~\ref{cor:compact-five-node-presentation-consequence}; its supplemental

The exhaustive support
ledger below supplies the axis map, certificate tuple, six acceptance predicates,
verifier input/output contract, acceptance exactness, finite-coordinate

interface, bad-subrecord normal form, weak-interface maximality classifier,
finite-coordinate no-overclaim rigidity, and master-spine support-coordinate
compression needed to prove that compact map.  The ledger/checklist

\paragraph{Notation and scope boundary.}
Here \(\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)\) abbreviates record-gate soundness on the
finite submitted surface \(S\), package \(P\), ledger \(L\), and dispatch table
\(\Gamma\).  The stronger-reading preorder \(c\preceq_{\Gamma}c^{+}\) means that
\(c^{+}\) asserts every finite coordinate of \(c\) and at least one additional
axis, evidence level, semantic, implementation, venue, or support coordinate
assigned by \(\Gamma\).  A finite bad subrecord is an inclusion-minimal subset of
the submitted finite fields that witnesses the first failed acceptance predicate.
A support-coordinate fixed point is a support tuple whose inventory bytes,
verifier inputs, verifier logs, and digest rows name one another at the same
source state.  A no-free-upgrade result says that a stronger reading is accepted
only after its positive finite coordinate is added and passed.

The supplement is deliberately limited to auditable theory-to-paper workflow
claims for formal mathematics.  It does not propose a theorem prover, a Lean
hammer, a complete BEDC theory, an automated journal-acceptance method, or a
claim that AI output is proof evidence.  Some logistical facts are stated in
proposition or theorem environments because they are finite-record consequences
used by the certificate calculus; those statements should be read as conditional
audit-record claims over printed paths, tables, manifests, and logs.  The
mathematical obligations are discharged by the displayed TeX definitions,
theorems, and proofs in the core chain, not by the theorem inventory, upload
support records, digest records, or venue-boundary records.

The weak-interface maximality and stronger-reading classifier machinery is used
here only as the finite-record audit calculus needed to protect the compact
presentation claim from overreading.  It is not split into an independent
audit-calculus article in this package.  A future paper could isolate that
classifier as a standalone finite-record audit calculus, but the present
manuscript uses it as support for the auditable auto-formalization method.

\begin{proposition}[Final package-shape convention]
\label{prop:final-package-shape-convention}
For the presentation package there is a single source-level package
shape.  The primary article is \path{submission_abstract.tex}; the submitted
technical supplement is \path{main.tex}; the bounded theorem-obligation ledger
consists of \path{theorem_inventory.json} and \path{theorem_inventory.md}; and
the source/support-package surface is the finite tuple
\path{theorem_inventory.json}, \path{theorem_inventory.md}, and
\path{review_bundle/} with the final digest record
\path{review_bundle/FINAL_DIGESTS_SHA256.md}.  The package records no
DOI-bearing replacement, venue-upload receipt, final archive-equivalent
byte-equality locator, or alternate external support directory.  Consequently
bundle-backed support claims in this source are source/package-verified finite
records, not public archive or venue-upload claims, unless a later finite upload
receipt or archive-equivalence byte-equality record is added.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The assertion is a finite record comparison.  The primary source names
\path{submission_abstract.tex} as the primary presentation article and states
that \path{main.tex}, \path{theorem_inventory.json},
\path{theorem_inventory.md}, and \path{review_bundle/} are submitted
source/support-package surfaces for the present route.  The opening package paragraph of this
supplement names the same coordinates and explicitly records that no venue-upload
receipt, DOI-bearing replacement, final archive-equivalent byte-equality locator,
or alternate external support directory is present.  The digest manifest
\path{review_bundle/FINAL_DIGESTS_SHA256.md} records the local finite byte table,
while the bundle manifest and support-boundary text record only candidate public
coordinates until byte equality is separately witnessed.  These finite source
records therefore agree on one package shape and one route-level support mode:
compact public article plus submitted technical source/support package.

It remains only to identify the boundary of the convention.  A source-level
package-shape record fixes which files the manuscript treats as primary,
supplemental, and support material; it does not by itself prove that a venue
upload has occurred or that an archive-equivalent locator has been instantiated.
Hence bundle-backed claims remain local/path-verified unless a later finite
coordinate supplies an upload receipt or locator-plus-byte-equality record for the
same digest-identified tuple.  Since the current finite records contain no DOI,
venue-upload receipt, or public byte-equality receipt, none of those stronger
records can be inferred from the source.  This proves both the single package
convention and its local-support boundary.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Nested six-row and seven-row package states]
\label{thm:nested-package-states}
Let $P^{+}_{6}$ denote the current row-frozen certificate state whose accepted
rows are exactly $a_1,\ldots,a_6$ in
Table~\ref{tab:current-acceptance-ledger}.  Let $P^{+}_{7}$ denote the enlarged
submitted support state obtained by adjoining the single theorem-ledger
row $a_7$ whose submitted coordinate is \path{theorem_inventory.json}.  Then
$P^{+}_{6}\subset P^{+}_{7}$ as finite record surfaces, and the inclusion is
conservative for the first six certificates: every acceptance decision, evidence
level, assigned-gate family, discovery-interface field, and command-boundary
field of rows $a_1,\ldots,a_6$ is the same in $P^{+}_{6}$ and $P^{+}_{7}$.  The
only new accepted claim of $P^{+}_{7}$ is the bounded theorem-obligation
ledger claim with syntactic label coverage for $a_7$.  In particular the two states are nested package states,
not competing final ledgers: $P^{+}_{6}$ is the exact six-row current-package
certificate state used by Theorem~\ref{thm:current-package-certificate-exactness},
while $P^{+}_{7}$ is the submitted theorem-ledger extension used by
Theorem~\ref{thm:theorem-obligation-ledger-boundary}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The tables and support records are finite, so the assertion is checked by
coordinates.  By definition, $P^{+}_{6}$ contains the primary article, this
supplement, the six accepted rows $a_1,\ldots,a_6$, their certificate fields, and
the conditional review-bundle support surface named in
Proposition~\ref{prop:current-package-acceptance-certificate-ledger}.  The state
$P^{+}_{7}$ is formed by adding one additional row, $a_7$, together with the
manifest exposure of \path{theorem_inventory.json}.  No row $a_i$ with
$1\leq i\leq 6$ is edited in this construction, and no field of its certificate
is replaced: the same finite tuple $(K_i,\ell_i,E_i,H_i,R_i,D_i,B_i)$ is read by
Definition~\ref{def:certificate-schema-acceptance-table} in both states.  Hence
Theorem~\ref{thm:record-acceptance-exactness} gives the same acceptance decision
for each of the six rows in both states.

The added coordinate has a different declared role.  Its accepted claim is not a
new mathematical proof, a proof-assistant rebuild, or an extractor-completeness
claim; it is the obligation-ledger traceability claim with syntactic label coverage
later classified in Proposition~\ref{prop:manual-theorem-inventory-boundary}.  Since the finite
record added to pass from $P^{+}_{6}$ to $P^{+}_{7}$ is exactly this new row and
its manifest exposure, every accepted claim outside $a_7$ is inherited unchanged
from $P^{+}_{6}$, while $a_7$ supplies only the bounded theorem-ledger coordinate.
This proves both the nesting and the non-competition statement.
\end{proof}

The setting is adjacent to proof-assistant systems such as Lean
\cite{deMouraKADR2015Lean}, machine-learning interfaces to formal proving such
as LeanDojo \cite{YangEtAl2023LeanDojo}, informal-to-formal guidance methods
such as Draft--Sketch--Prove \cite{JiangEtAl2023DraftSketchProve}, and
large-scale formal-proof archives such as the Archive of Formal Proofs
\cite{BlanchetteHMN2015AFP}.  Our focus is different: we study the
publication-facing evidence discipline around such sources.

\section{Architecture}

The workflow separates source work from publication work, and the separation is
the organizing contract for the rest of the supplement.  BEDC source files are
treated as finite-kernel theory together with proof obligations and separate
implementation contracts.  Lean and related markers are formal-verification
records for named obligations, not object-language closure by themselves.
Finite manifests, evaluator rows, bundled snapshots, and command logs are the
substrate witnesses from which publication certificates are built.  AI agents
remain advisory: they may propose, review, and triage, but they do not promote
claims into accepted theory.  The automath layer is therefore a publication
compiler: it packages the source-theory interface, finite witnesses, route state,
and submission boundary without merging those evidence axes.

This file is technical supplementary support for the public presentation article

\ref{thm:six-role-publication-master-interface},
Corollary~\ref{cor:primary-presentation-weak-interface-compression},
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-script-projection-contract-support},
Proposition~\ref{prop:presentation-case-matrix-sufficiency}, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-row-case-evidence-closure}.  Later theorem, proposition,

they unpack finite tables, projection contracts, bad-subrecord classifications,

\begin{definition}[Architecture-axis map]
\label{def:architecture-axis-map}
The compiler architecture uses five disjoint evidence axes.  An accepted claim may
read evidence from an axis only at the admissible evidence level shown in
the displayed axis map; the negative boundary in the last column
is part of the claim certificate and cannot be discharged by prose from another
axis.
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{p{.16\textwidth}p{.27\textwidth}p{.27\textwidth}X}
\toprule
Axis & Role in this paper & Admissible evidence & Negative boundary \\
\midrule
BEDC source theory & finite-kernel theory, proof obligations, and implementation
contracts & pinned source paths, commits, imported labels, bounded summaries, and
source-interface records & not a publication acceptance record, not a fresh rebuild,
and not a complete BEDC exposition \\
Lean markers & formal-verification records for named obligations & recorded build,
axiom-purity, marker-existence, or source-interface rows when named by the package &
not object-language closure, not discovery by itself, and not proof of unrelated
claims \\
Finite witnesses & manifest/evaluator substrate evidence for artifacts and package
certificates & manifest rows, evaluator outcomes, bundled snapshots, verifier logs,
file digests, and limitation ledgers & not semantic universality, not whole-tree
dynamic validation, and not an unbounded artifact rerun \\
Agents & proposal, search, review, ranking, and repair assistance & advisory drafts,
review reports, scheduler scores, and gate-input suggestions after being recorded
as such & not proof evidence, not human promotion, not novelty certification, and
not gate passage \\
Automath publication compiler & intake, route, overlap, submission-pack, and support
surface governance & promotion records, active-paper markers, overlap ledgers,
submission-interface maps, digest manifests, command logs, and upload-or-archive
records when present & not the whole mathematical contribution, not venue
acceptance, and not authority to merge evidence axes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Axis non-escalation]
\label{prop:architecture-axis-non-escalation}
In any record-gate-sound package using Definition~\ref{def:architecture-axis-map},
passage or evidence on one architecture axis cannot certify a load-bearing claim
whose claim kind requires another axis.  More precisely, if a claim certificate
uses an axis $A$ but its stronger reading needs an evidence item or negative-boundary
discharge listed only on a different axis $A'$, then the stronger reading is not
accepted unless the package contains a separate submitted coordinate for $A'$ and
the gates assigned to that coordinate pass.  Consequently
Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} constructs only finite publication
certificates whose axis coordinates are explicitly present in the submitted support
surface; it does not infer BEDC closure from Lean markers, artifact semantics from
manifest rows, proof evidence from agents, venue upload from automath route state,
or support-surface availability from local bundle paths.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The operational interface records a claim by finite coordinates: claim kind,
evidence surface, evidence level, pass records assigned by $\Gamma$, and the
boundary field.  Definition~\ref{def:architecture-axis-map} makes the axis of each
such coordinate explicit and declares the corresponding negative boundary.  If a
stronger reading needs an item on a different axis $A'$, then either the claim-kind
coordinate does not name the kind requiring $A'$, the evidence surface does not
contain an admissible $A'$ item, a required $A'$ pass record is missing, or the
boundary field still excludes the stronger reading.  In all four cases the finite
record verifier of Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-certificate-schema-verifier}
rejects the stronger reading: the dispatch table cannot assign an unmentioned gate,
the surface check cannot read an unsubmitted path or log, the pass-record check
cannot be satisfied without the row, and the boundary check preserves the declared
negative boundary.

Conversely, when a separate coordinate for $A'$ is submitted, it is just another
finite component of the package.  It can be accepted only by the same schema:
its claim kind must dispatch to the appropriate gates, its evidence surface must
list the admissible $A'$ evidence, and its boundary must state exactly what is and
is not certified.  Therefore evidence never moves between axes by paraphrase or by
agent-generated text; it moves only by adding an explicit finite coordinate and
passing the assigned gates.  Applying this to the five rows of
Definition~\ref{def:architecture-axis-map} gives the listed consequences.  They are
also the axis-level instance of the coordinate-determination result later isolated
in Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-coordinate-determination-boundary}: facts outside the
finite coordinates of the accepted package are not conclusions of the certificate.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Conditional RGS finite-record public spine theorem]
\label{thm:presentation-compressed-interface}
Fix a presentation-only package whose architecture axes are those of
Definition~\ref{def:architecture-axis-map}.  Suppose its load-bearing claims are
checked only through the finite submitted surface $S$, acceptance ledger $L$,
dispatch table $\Gamma$, and verifier tuple
\(\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)\) of
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}, and suppose the package
satisfies the record-gate-soundness hypothesis used in
Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface}.  Then its whole presentation
claim factors through the following five-coordinate interface:
\[
\Pi_{\mathrm{pres}}(S,L,\Gamma)=
\bigl(\mathsf{Axis},\mathsf{RGS},\mathsf{Cert},
\mathsf{Bad},\mathsf{Boundary}\bigr),
\]
where \(\mathsf{Axis}\) is the five-axis map,
\(\mathsf{RGS}\) is the finite record-gate-soundness predicate,
\(\mathsf{Cert}\) is the accepted finite certificate set
\(\mathsf{Out}_{\Gamma,S}(L)\), \(\mathsf{Bad}\) is the finite bad-subrecord
report, and \(\mathsf{Boundary}\) is the list of negative boundaries printed in
Definition~\ref{def:architecture-axis-map} together with the command-run and
support-coordinate boundary fields in \(B\).  Under the same explicit accepted
record-gate-soundness row or hypothesis, this projection is complete only for
the finite-record CICM software-architecture reading of the paper, as classified
by Theorem~\ref{thm:presentation-route-dichotomy}, and is sharp against stronger
readings in the following finite-record sense: every primary load-bearing
assertion must factor through this projection together with
Corollary~\ref{cor:primary-presentation-weak-interface-compression}, while the local round,
digest, inventory, and script labels retained in the supplement are proof
pullbacks and not separate primary theorem surface.  More precisely:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The compact presentation may assert the typed architecture, the advisory
status of agents, the finite certificate output, and the finite bad-subrecord
obstruction using only \(\Pi_{\mathrm{pres}}\).
\item It may use imported BEDC labels only as bounded source-interface rows; it
does not thereby assert semantic truth of the imported BEDC theorems, a Lean
rebuild, or an axiom audit for this package.
\item It may use the case-study rows only as path-verified or historical finite
witnesses unless the relevant current command-run, daemon, evaluator, or artifact
rerun coordinates are also included in \(S\) and passed by their assigned gates.
\item It may use venue and bibliography records only as dated planning or
freshness coordinates unless the upload, archive-equivalence, or upload-time venue
compliance coordinates are also included in \(S\) and passed by their assigned
gates.
\item Any stronger reading that adds semantic BEDC truth, gate implementation
soundness, fresh daemon behavior, dynamic artifact validation, upload receipt,
archive locator, or venue acceptance is accepted by the same interface if and
only if the corresponding finite extension coordinate is added to $S$ and the
enlarged record passes the assigned gates.  If it is not added, the stronger
reading is rejected by a finite bad subrecord while the compressed presentation
claim remains unchanged.  Thus this is a finite-record software-method schema:
the executable or reviewer-checkable objects are records, projections, verifier
predicates, and bad-subrecord reports, not a new proof method for the underlying
BEDC mathematics or an implementation-correctness theorem for the workflow
programs.
\end{enumerate}
Thus the labelled theorem ledger retained in this supplement is an expansion of
the support proof, not a second reviewer-facing contribution competing with the
compressed architecture theorem.  More precisely, after applying the projection
\(\Pi_{\mathrm{pres}}\), every labelled theorem-like environment in the supplement
belongs to exactly one of the following public roles: the six-role architecture
interface, the conditional RGS publication-safety interface, the finite-record
classifier and bad-subrecord calculus, the finite-script projection-contract
support interface, one of the four path-complete case-row skeletons, or an
internal proof pullback for one of those roles.  Hence the primary compact
presentation article has the forced exposed theorem surface
\[
  \bigl\{
  \ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface},
  \ref{thm:portable-six-role-interface},
  \ref{thm:publication-safety-interface},
  \ref{thm:compact-article-finite-record-spine-classification},
  \ref{thm:finite-script-projection-contract-support},
  \ref{prop:path-complete-case-witnesses}
  \bigr\},
\]
where the last entry is read as the four case-row skeletons named in
Section~\ref{sec:gate-summary}.  Every other theorem, proposition, lemma, or
corollary in this technical supplement is admissible in the public article only
as a cited proof-support coordinate for one of these six roles and not as a
separate reviewer-facing theorem surface.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The displayed tuple is finite because Definition~\ref{def:architecture-axis-map}
has five rows, $\Gamma$ has the finite domain printed in
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}, and each certificate
\(\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)\) has seven finite fields.  Under the stated
record-gate-soundness hypothesis, Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface}
constructs exactly the accepted set
\(\mathsf{Out}_{\Gamma,S}(L)\) and the finite list of rejected bad subrecords from
these fields.  The same theorem proves maximality for the stronger-reading
preorder: a strengthened claim is accepted precisely when the finite coordinate
that expresses the strengthening is present and has passing assigned gates; if
that coordinate is absent, the first missing field is a finite bad subrecord.

It remains only to identify which coordinates are visible in the presentation
projection.  Clause~1 is the positive part of
Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface}: it outputs finite certificates
and finite bad-subrecord reports from the submitted surface, ledger, dispatch
table, and verifier.  Proposition~\ref{prop:architecture-axis-non-escalation}
shows that evidence on one axis cannot discharge a claim assigned to another
axis.  Therefore the negative boundaries in the axis map are preserved in the
projection and cannot be removed by shortening the article.  Applying this
non-escalation to the BEDC source-theory axis gives clause~2; the admissible
coordinate is the pinned source-interface row, while semantic theorem truth,
Lean rebuild correctness, and axiom audit live on stronger coordinates not
present in that row.  Applying it to the finite-witness and automath axes gives
clauses~3 and~4: historical witness rows, manifest rows, route records, and dated
venue checks are admissible only at the evidence level recorded in $S$, and a
fresh execution, evaluator semantics, upload receipt, archive coordinate, or
upload-time venue certificate requires its own finite coordinate.

Clause~5 is exactly the sharpness statement just recalled from
Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface}, specialized to the stronger
readings named in clauses~2--4.  Since all accepted presentation claims and all
rejected stronger readings are determined by
\(\Pi_{\mathrm{pres}}(S,L,\Gamma)\), replacing the expanded theorem ledger by a
compact statement of this tuple preserves the presentation contribution.  The
six displayed public roles are forced as follows.  The present theorem supplies
the compressed public projection.  The portable six-role theorem is the unique
role factorisation of an accepted finite certificate.  The publication-safety
theorem supplies the conditional RGS certificate construction and checker
exactness.  The compact-spine classification theorem partitions the remaining
labelled support calculus into primary-spine and support-only coordinates.  The
finite-script projection-contract theorem states exactly what the named scripts
certify from their finite parsed inputs.  Finally,
Proposition~\ref{prop:path-complete-case-witnesses} is the classifier for the
four case-row skeletons in Section~\ref{sec:gate-summary}.  Each remaining
labelled environment in this file either refines one of those six roles,
instantiates it for the current local package, or records a boundary preventing a
stronger reading from being glued to it.  Promoting such a local label to the
primary article would therefore add notation without adding a new accepted
coordinate.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Compact-presentation boundary routing]
\label{cor:compact-presentation-boundary-routing}
In the CICM presentation-only article associated with this supplement, the
results
\[
\begin{gathered}
\text{Theorems~\ref{thm:finite-script-projection-contract-support},
\ref{thm:six-coordinate-gate-implementation-soundness-skeleton},
\ref{thm:finite-certificate-obstruction-skeleton},}\
\text{Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-witness-manifest-record-interface},
Proposition~\ref{prop:artifact-validation-gate-unique-semantic-upgrade},
Corollary~\ref{cor:artifact-semantic-validity-boundary},}\
\text{and Theorems~\ref{thm:current-inventory-artifact-realization},
\ref{thm:current-command-result-closure}}
\end{gathered}
\]
can be cited only through the projection
\(\Pi_{\mathrm{pres}}(S,L,\Gamma)\) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface}.  Consequently the compact
article has the following forced normal form.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Script rows assert only the finite predicates printed by the retained
record-checking scripts; they do not certify object-language mathematics,
proof-assistant correctness, or all gate implementations.
\item Gate and obstruction skeletons are boundary interfaces for missing finite
coordinates; they are not implementation-soundness theorems for the underlying
programs.
\item Manifest and evaluator-witness rows assert only manifest-bounded finite
witnesses unless fresh evaluator or artifact-validation logs are submitted and
assigned passing rows.
\item Inventory, digest, and command-result rows assert only local/path-verified
support for the named source bytes and logs; they are not clean-machine
reproducibility, external-upload, archive-equivalence, or venue-acceptance
claims.
\item The publication-audit conclusion is always conditional on the four
hypotheses printed in Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface}, especially
record-gate soundness and the finite submitted certificates present in the
package.
\end{enumerate}
Any compact statement violating one of these five clauses is a proper stronger
reading and is rejected by the same finite bad-subrecord mechanism while the
bounded presentation claim remains accepted.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface} proves that every
presentation claim factors through the finite tuple
\(\Pi_{\mathrm{pres}}(S,L,\Gamma)\) and that stronger readings are accepted only
after the corresponding finite extension coordinate is added and passes its
assigned gates.  Each labelled result listed in the statement refines one of the
finite axes or boundary fields of that tuple.  The concrete-script theorem and
its instantiation corollary refine the command-run and script-projection field;
their statement explicitly limits exit code zero to the parsed finite predicate.
The six-coordinate and finite-certificate skeleton theorems refine the bad
subrecord field; by construction they identify missing implementation,
certificate, or evidence coordinates rather than proving those coordinates.
The finite-witness interface, artifact-validation gate proposition, and semantic
validity boundary corollary refine the finite-witness axis; their positive field
is the manifest or evaluator row, and dynamic semantic validation is an added
coordinate.  The current-inventory and command-result closure theorems refine the
local support and command-boundary fields; their positive data are named local
bytes, paths, source states, exit codes, logs, and digest rows.

Clauses~1--4 are exactly these four projections read with the negative-boundary
component of \(\Pi_{\mathrm{pres}}\).  Clause~5 is the headline hypothesis list of
Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface}: without those hypotheses the
finite certificate map is not asserted, and with them it remains an interface
theorem for submitted rows rather than a global pipeline-safety theorem.  If a
compact sentence asserts object-language mathematics, all gate implementation
soundness, dynamic artifact validation, clean-machine reproducibility, external
upload, or unconditional pipeline correctness, it adds an architecture-axis,
evidence-level, command-run, implementation, artifact, venue, or semantic
coordinate not present in the projection.  The sharpness clause of
Theorem~\ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface}, equivalently the maximality
part of Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface}, then gives a finite bad
subrecord for the added coordinate.  The original bounded presentation claim
uses only the projected tuple and is therefore unchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Public-result support-surface rigidity]
\label{thm:public-result-support-surface-rigidity}
For the CICM presentation-only route, let
\[
\mathcal H=\{\ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface}\}
\]
be the headline theorem surface and let \(\mathcal S\) be the set of all labelled
theorem-like statements in this supplement whose conclusions mention a local
round, digest, inventory, command log, case snapshot, finite-script row,
source-interface row, master spine, weak interface, upload/archive coordinate, or
support-coordinate classifier.  Then every compact-paper load-bearing citation to
\(\mathcal S\) factors through Theorem~\ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface}
by one of the five coordinates of \(\Pi_{\mathrm{pres}}(S,L,\Gamma)\).  Moreover
this routing is rigid: replacing \(\mathcal H\) by \(\mathcal H\cup T\) for any
\(T\in\mathcal S\) as an additional headline result either adds no accepted finite
coordinate, in which case it is a notational duplicate of the same projection, or
adds a stronger reading and is rejected until the corresponding finite upgrade
coordinate is submitted and passed.  Thus the compact article has exactly one
public theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface}; the
portable six-role, publication-safety, finite-script, source-interface,
case-snapshot, master-spine, and compact-classification results are support
lemmas, propositions, theorems, and corollaries for that public theorem.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface}, every accepted
presentation claim is a function of the finite tuple
\(\Pi_{\mathrm{pres}}(S,L,\Gamma)=(\mathsf{Axis},\mathsf{RGS},\mathsf{Cert},
\mathsf{Bad},\mathsf{Boundary})\).  The proof of that theorem identifies the
local round, digest, inventory, script, case, source-interface, and venue labels
as proof pullbacks for these five fields rather than independent primary axes.
Corollary~\ref{cor:compact-presentation-boundary-routing} then classifies the
script, implementation, witness, inventory, and publication-audit labels by the
same projection and states the negative boundary attached to each class.

Let \(T\in\mathcal S\).  If the conclusion of \(T\) asserts only one of the finite
fields already present in \(\Pi_{\mathrm{pres}}\), then citing \(T\) in the compact
article is merely a proof expansion of the relevant coordinate; promoting it to
the headline theorem surface does not change the accepted certificate set or the
bad-subrecord report.  If instead the promoted reading of \(T\) asserts something
outside those five fields, then it changes an architecture axis, raises an
evidence level, or adds a semantic, implementation, artifact, venue, or support
coordinate.  The sharpness clause of
Theorem~\ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface} and the extension criterion in
Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} say that such a reading is accepted
if and only if that finite coordinate is added to the submitted surface and its
assigned gates pass; otherwise the first missing coordinate is returned as a
finite bad subrecord.  These two cases exhaust all labelled support statements by
the definition of \(\mathcal S\), proving both factorization and rigidity.
\end{proof}

The reader path is therefore architectural before it is logistical.  The rest of
the supplement first fixes the source-interface spine, then defines the finite
record verifier, then proves the certificate construction and non-escalation
boundary, then instantiates that boundary on the current six-row package, and
only then lists the local case snapshots and command-run inventory.  File tables
are included as finite witnesses for this interface, not as a substitute for the
compiler architecture.

Concretely, the newmath source workspace contains Lean files, scripts, and
artifact sources.  The automath publication workspace contains intake packets,
active paper tracks, review state, and submission metadata.  A candidate first
enters an intake seed.  It becomes an active paper only after a human promotion
decision creates a \texttt{2026\_*} directory with \texttt{main.tex} and
\texttt{PIPELINE.md}.  This prevents source organization from being mistaken for
a submission route.

The source side supplies a discovery-gate calculus.  In this calculus,
statement-only and code-only candidates are insufficient; mechanical expansion
and compression are not discovery by themselves; discovery claims require a
semantic certificate and a ledger witness; demotion preserves source-interface
audit soundness;
accepted claims must form an auditable lineage DAG; and a pipeline is safe only
when discovery claims pass the gate before being recorded as accepted work.

\begin{proposition}[Manual source-interface non-escalation]
\label{prop:manual-source-interface-non-escalation}
Let $I$ be the imported discovery-gate interface certified by
Lemma~\ref{lem:source-interface-extraction-correctness}.  Any later use of an
imported source label in this paper is a consequence of $I$ only if it is a
function of the finite fields recorded in Table~\ref{tab:source-interface-record}:
the source path, pinned commit, label, line range, extraction date, bounded
summary, and evidence-level qualifier.  A proposed stronger use---for example an
exact import of the original source theorem statement, a fresh BEDC or Lean
rebuild, an axiom-purity statement, or a semantic validation of the imported
source theorem---is accepted by the finite-record safety interface only after the
submitted record surface is enlarged by the corresponding source-statement,
formal-build, or command-run coordinate and by the assigned pass records for that
coordinate.  Without that enlargement the stronger use is rejected as a finite
bad subrecord and the accepted consequence remains the manual path-verified
bounded interface.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{lem:source-interface-extraction-correctness} identifies exactly the
finite fields in $I$ and states that the summaries are bounded paraphrases rather
than replacements of the original source statements.  Therefore two possible
review states that agree on those fields but differ in an unsubmitted source
checkout, proof-assistant state, axiom audit, or executable extraction log give
the same values to every coordinate read by $I$.  By
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-coordinate-determination-boundary}, no claim depending on
one of the differing unsubmitted coordinates is a consequence of the finite
interface record.

If a stronger use is made load-bearing, then it strictly enlarges the original
source-interface reading in the stronger-reading preorder of
Definition~\ref{def:stronger-reading-preorder}: exact source-statement import
adds an evidence-surface coordinate, a BEDC or Lean rebuild adds formal-source or
command-run coordinates, axiom-purity adds an assigned gate and pass record, and
semantic validation adds a new claim-kind or boundary coordinate.  The normal
form of Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-extension-budget-normal-form} says that such a
genuine strengthening is accepted exactly when the added finite coordinates and
their gate records are supplied.  If they are absent,
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-certificate-obstruction-skeleton} returns the missing
coordinate as a finite bad subrecord.  Thus the source import used downstream,
including in Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface}, remains the manual
path-verified bounded interface and nothing stronger.\end{proof}

\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The proposition is a finite equality-and-containment check over submitted
records.  The script \path{review_bundle/verify_source_interface_record.py}
parses the sixteen rows of Table~\ref{tab:source-interface-record} from this source,
loads \path{source_interface_record.json}, loads the
\path{pinned_source_snapshot} object of
\path{review_bundle/REVIEW_BUNDLE_MANIFEST.json}, and computes the SHA-256 digest
and line count of the bundled snapshot.  It then checks seven finite conditions:
the ordered manuscript rows are the ordered JSON records; the JSON source path
and commit equal the manifest's original path and commit; the ordered JSON line
ranges equal the manifest's \path{line_ranges_used}; the computed digest equals
the manifest digest; the computed line count equals the manifest line count; and for each declared range,
the corresponding \path{\label{...}} token occurs inside that inclusive snapshot
interval.

The recorded run in \path{review_bundle/source_interface_verification_run.log}
has status \path{pass}.  Its counts are sixteen manuscript table rows, sixteen JSON
records, sixteen manifest ranges, snapshot line count 498, and digest
\path{a492900222dd66d154cdd5a79d2b2ed0b856ad1ec59e5dfce55dbc21875ed1b2}.  Its
\path{imported_newmath_source_commit} field is the external source commit
\path{3fb3d6a0641767388a401883062aa522ea0b397b}; its
\path{local_publication_package_commit} field is only provenance for the local
paper checkout used to run the verifier and is not a second imported-source pin.  Its
per-row label checks all report \path{label_in_range: true} for the sixteen labels
listed in Table~\ref{tab:source-interface-record}.  Therefore no accepted row can
be a table-only, JSON-only, manifest-only, or out-of-range source-interface row:
any such defect would violate one of the seven checked finite conditions and would
appear as a finite bad subrecord.  What remains unchecked is exactly outside the
claim: the script does not interpret or prove the imported theorem statements,
does not check BEDC semantic extraction, and does not check Lean or source-theory
completeness.  The manuscript does not quote the imported statements as exact
source theorem text.  The exact source text remains available only as the bundled
snapshot at the displayed line ranges.  Thus the executable comparison strengthens
the earlier manual audit into a reproducible equality-and-containment certificate
while preserving the bounded-paraphrase and non-semantic boundary.\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Bounded source-interface maximality]
\label{thm:bounded-source-interface-maximality}
Let $I_{\rm man}$ be the manual imported-source interface of
Lemma~\ref{lem:source-interface-extraction-correctness}, and let $I_{\rm exe}$
be the executable finite comparison of
Proposition~\ref{prop:source-interface-record-file-consistency}.  In the
finite-record safety interface of Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface},
the strongest imported discovery-gate premise available from
$I_{\rm man}$ together with $I_{\rm exe}$ is exactly the following finite
certificate:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the imported source path and pinned source commit;
\item the sixteen ordered labels, line ranges, extraction date, and bounded
statement summaries in Table~\ref{tab:source-interface-record};
\item equality of those ordered triples with \path{source_interface_record.json};
\item agreement with the review-bundle manifest on source path, source commit,
line ranges, snapshot digest, and snapshot line count; and
\item containment of each imported label token in its declared bundled-snapshot
line interval.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently every accepted use of an imported discovery-gate label in the main
theorem chain, in particular in Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface},
factors through this finite certificate.  Any reading that imports the exact
source theorem statements, asserts semantic truth of the imported theorems,
performs a BEDC or Lean rebuild, proves axiom purity, or certifies source-theory
completeness is a properly stronger reading and is rejected unless the submitted
surface is enlarged by the corresponding finite source-statement, command-run,
formal-build, axiom-audit, or semantic-check coordinate and by its assigned pass
records.  In particular, stronger formal-source claims require fresh
formal-source rows naming the exact source text or build command, source state,
environment, exit code, log path, digest binding, and assigned pass row; they are
not supplied by the bounded path/label/summary interface.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{lem:source-interface-extraction-correctness} supplies exactly the
manual finite fields in (1) and (2), and it states that the row summaries are
bounded paraphrases rather than replacements for the full source statements.
Proposition~\ref{prop:source-interface-record-file-consistency} supplies exactly
the executable finite fields in (3)--(5): the script compares the manuscript
table, JSON mirror, bundle manifest, digest, line count, and labelled intervals
and reports a finite bad subrecord on any failed comparison.  These two records
therefore have the displayed union as their complete positive content.

The verifier used in Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} can read only
submitted finite coordinates.  By Proposition~\ref{prop:manual-source-interface-non-escalation},
Proposition~\ref{prop:source-interface-evidence-level-separation}, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-coordinate-determination-boundary}, two review states
that agree on the displayed finite certificate but differ in an unsubmitted
source checkout, proof-assistant state, axiom audit, semantic extractor, or build
log are indistinguishable to the imported-source component of the certificate
constructor.  Hence every accepted imported-label premise in the theorem chain
factors through the displayed certificate.

Each excluded reading strictly adds a finite coordinate in the preorder of
Definition~\ref{def:stronger-reading-preorder}: exact source-statement import
adds a source-text evidence coordinate; BEDC or Lean rebuilding adds a formal
source or command-run coordinate; axiom purity adds an audit coordinate and pass
row; and semantic source-theorem validation adds a semantic-check coordinate.
Fresh formal-source strength is therefore a separate row type, not a refinement
of the bounded paraphrase row.  The finite extension-budget normal form,
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-extension-budget-normal-form}, accepts such a stronger
reading exactly when those added coordinates and pass records are present.
When they are absent, Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-certificate-obstruction-skeleton}
classifies the missing coordinate as a finite bad subrecord.  Thus the displayed
certificate is maximal for the submitted source-interface surface while remaining
strictly bounded to record equality and label containment.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Downstream imported-label use factors through bounded rows]
\label{cor:downstream-imported-label-bounded-factorization}
Every load-bearing occurrence in this manuscript of an imported discovery-gate
label from Table~\ref{tab:source-interface-record} factors through the bounded
source-interface certificate of
Theorem~\ref{thm:bounded-source-interface-maximality}.  Hence a downstream proof
may use only the row's recorded path, pinned commit, label token, line range,
extraction date, bounded summary, evidence-level qualifier, equality with
\path{source_interface_record.json}, manifest agreement, and bundled-snapshot
label containment.  If such an occurrence is read instead as an exact quotation
of the source theorem, as a semantic import of its proof, or as a source-theory
rebuild claim, the reading is a properly stronger source-interface claim and is
not accepted without the corresponding added coordinates and pass records.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:bounded-source-interface-maximality} identifies the maximal
finite certificate available from the manual row audit together with the
executable comparison.  The only imported labels available to later proofs are
the sixteen rows of Table~\ref{tab:source-interface-record}, by
Lemma~\ref{lem:source-interface-extraction-correctness}; and
Proposition~\ref{prop:manual-source-interface-non-escalation} says that any later
consequence of that interface must be a function of exactly those finite fields.
Thus every downstream occurrence factors through the displayed bounded
certificate.  A reading that imports an exact statement, a semantic proof, or a
source-theory rebuild adds a source-statement, semantic, formal-build, or
command-run coordinate absent from the certificate.  By
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-extension-budget-normal-form} such a strengthening is
accepted exactly when the added coordinates and assigned pass records are
present; otherwise Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-certificate-obstruction-skeleton}
returns the missing coordinate as a finite bad subrecord.  This proves both the
factorization and the non-escalation clause.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Public-source reachability non-escalation]
\label{thm:public-source-reachability-non-escalation}
In the current source package, the bounded-source citation \cite{bedc-newmath-source} and the
commit string \path{3fb3d6a0641767388a401883062aa522ea0b397b} serve only as the
public-source coordinate for the imported newmath workspace.  The load-bearing
source-interface premise used by Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface}
remains the bundled finite record certified by
Theorem~\ref{thm:bounded-source-interface-maximality}: path, commit string,
sixteen labels, line ranges, bounded summaries, JSON equality, manifest agreement,
snapshot digest and line count, and label containment in the bundled snapshot.
Unless the submitted surface additionally contains a dated public-repository
reachability and byte-equality log for the pinned commit and bundled snapshot, no
claim in this paper may infer that the public repository was reachable at review
time, that the public branch contains the pinned commit, or that public bytes are
equal to the bundled snapshot bytes.  If such a dated log is added, its only
upgrade is the finite reachability/equality coordinate named by that log; it still
does not prove semantic truth of the imported source theorems, Lean/BEDC rebuild
success, marker correctness, or axiom purity.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:bounded-source-interface-maximality} identifies the complete
positive imported-source content currently supplied to the finite-record safety
theorem: it is a finite bundle-backed equality-and-containment certificate over
the manuscript table, \path{source_interface_record.json}, the review-bundle
manifest, and the bundled source snapshot.  None of those fields is a dated
network observation.  In particular, a commit string in a citation and a local
snapshot digest are not fields recording a public-repository command, remote URL,
environment, exit code, log path, fetched object identity, or byte comparison
against a public checkout.

Consider two review states that agree on every field listed in
Theorem~\ref{thm:bounded-source-interface-maximality} and on the bibliography
entry \cite{bedc-newmath-source}.  In the first state a reviewer also has a dated
successful remote-reachability and byte-equality log; in the second state that log
is absent.  The current verifier and theorem chain read the same finite
coordinates in both states, because the distinguishing public-reachability log is
not part of the submitted support surface.  By
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-coordinate-determination-boundary}, a stronger conclusion
that distinguishes these states cannot be inferred from the common finite tuple.
Thus public reachability, public commit containment, and public byte equality are
not current consequences of the citation or bundled snapshot records.

If a later package adds the dated log, then the support tuple has a new finite
coordinate: the command or check performed, the public repository locator, the
source commit, the compared path or object, the environment, the exit code, the
log path, and the resulting digest or equality record.  The finite extension is
accepted exactly as an added coordinate under
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-extension-budget-normal-form}; it does not add any of the
separate semantic, formal-build, marker, or axiom-audit coordinates excluded by
Theorem~\ref{thm:source-interface-semantic-completeness-obstruction}.  Hence the
only possible upgrade is the stated finite public reachability/equality reading.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Public-source coordinate exactness]
\label{cor:public-source-coordinate-exactness}
For the present source package, any load-bearing statement containing the public
source citation \cite{bedc-newmath-source} and the pinned commit
\path{3fb3d6a0641767388a401883062aa522ea0b397b} factors through exactly the
bounded coordinates of Theorem~\ref{thm:public-source-reachability-non-escalation}.
Thus the citation contributes only the public locator, pinned commit string, and
the already-recorded bundled source-interface rows.  It contributes neither a
dated public fetch, nor a branch-membership proof, nor public byte equality, nor
semantic validity of the imported statements.  A public-source reading is
upgraded if and only if the submitted support surface adds a finite
fetch-and-compare coordinate naming the remote locator, object or commit, compared
path, source state, environment, exit code, log path, and resulting byte or digest
comparison.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:public-source-reachability-non-escalation} proves the negative
direction: the current finite tuple lacks the dated remote observation and byte
comparison fields, so public reachability, branch containment, and public byte
equality are not consequences of the citation or bundled snapshot.  The only
positive fields that remain are precisely the fields already read by
Theorem~\ref{thm:bounded-source-interface-maximality}: public locator as a
bibliographic coordinate, pinned commit string, source path, labels, line ranges,
bounded summaries, manifest agreement, snapshot digest and line count, and label
containment in the bundled snapshot.

For the converse upgrade criterion, suppose the submitted surface is enlarged by
the stated fetch-and-compare coordinate and by its assigned pass row.  That is a
finite extension coordinate in the sense of
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-extension-budget-normal-form}, so the certificate may now
read exactly the remote-reachability and byte/digest-comparison fact recorded in
that row.  No other field is added: semantic source validity, Lean/BEDC rebuild
success, marker correctness, and axiom purity would require separate semantic,
formal-build, marker, or axiom-audit coordinates.  Hence the factorisation and
the ``if and only if'' upgrade criterion are exact.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Source-interface semantic-completeness obstruction]
\label{thm:source-interface-semantic-completeness-obstruction}
Under the source-interface surface certified by
Lemma~\ref{lem:source-interface-extraction-correctness} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:bounded-source-interface-maximality}, every accepted imported
discovery-gate premise factors through the five finite fields listed in
Theorem~\ref{thm:bounded-source-interface-maximality}.  In particular, no theorem
in the main publication-safety chain may infer semantic completeness of the
imported source theory, correctness of the bounded summaries as exact source
statements, Lean/BEDC rebuild success, marker correctness, or axiom purity from
that surface.  A package claim with any one of those stronger meanings is
accepted by the same finite-record calculus if and only if the support surface is
extended by a nonempty machine-readable source-interface coordinate appropriate
to the stronger meaning: exact source-text import requires the exact source text
and a byte-equality or digest-binding comparison against the pinned snapshot;
public-source readings require a public fetch-and-compare record with byte
equality; formal-source readings require a Lean/BEDC rebuild record with command,
source state, environment, exit code, log path, and assigned pass row; and semantic
source-theory readings require a semantic-validation record naming the checker or
evaluator contract, produced record, digest binding, and assigned pass row.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $F(I)$ denote the finite projection consisting of the five fields displayed
in Theorem~\ref{thm:bounded-source-interface-maximality}.  That theorem proves
that $F(I)$ is the strongest positive imported-source premise available to
Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} from the submitted manual and
executable source-interface records.  Therefore any accepted consequence using
an imported discovery-gate label is a function of $F(I)$.

Now consider any stronger semantic reading, for instance exact source-statement
import or marker correctness.  There are two possible review states with the
same $F(I)$: in both states the path, commit, labels, line ranges, bounded
summaries, JSON equality, bundle-manifest agreement, digest row, line count, and
label containment checks agree; in one state an additional semantic extractor or
proof checker succeeds, while in the other no such command has been submitted or
the unsubmitted semantic fact is false.  The finite source-interface verifier
cannot distinguish these states because the distinguishing coordinate is not in
$F(I)$.  By Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-coordinate-determination-boundary} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:manual-source-interface-non-escalation}, the stronger
semantic conclusion is therefore not a consequence of the current interface.

Conversely, if the support surface is enlarged by the relevant finite coordinate
listed in the statement and by its assigned pass row, the enlarged coordinate is
no longer invisible to the certificate calculus: it becomes an ordinary finite
extension of the tuple read by the verifier.  Exact source text is then read only
through the submitted text and byte-comparison row; public reachability only
through the public fetch-and-compare row; rebuild success only through the
formal-build command row; and semantic validity only through the submitted
semantic-validation contract and produced record.  The acceptance of the
strengthened source-interface reading is therefore exactly the extension case of
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-extension-budget-normal-form}, applied to the enlarged
support surface.  Because at least one source-text, byte-equality,
formal-rebuild, semantic-validation, digest-binding, or pass-row field is added,
the extension is nonempty.  This proves both the obstruction and the stated
if-and-only-if upgrade criterion.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Source-interface evidence-level separation]
\label{prop:source-interface-evidence-level-separation}
Let $r$ be any accepted manuscript claim whose discovery component cites one of
the imported labels in Table~\ref{tab:source-interface-record}.  If $r$ uses only
Lemma~\ref{lem:source-interface-extraction-correctness}, then the imported-label
premise of $r$ is accepted only at the manual path-verified bounded-paraphrase
level.  If $r$ additionally cites
Proposition~\ref{prop:source-interface-record-file-consistency}, then the same
premise is upgraded only by the finite record comparisons listed in that
proposition: table--JSON equality, manifest agreement, snapshot digest and line
count agreement, and label containment in the declared ranges.  In neither case
does the premise become a fresh Lean/BEDC rebuild, a proof of the semantic truth
of the imported source theorem, or an unbounded restatement of the source text.
Consequently the finite-record interface theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface}, can use the imported
discovery-gate spine only through these two explicitly separated evidence
levels.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The operational evidence level of a cited source-interface premise is determined
by the record fields actually available for that premise.  Lemma~\ref{lem:source-interface-extraction-correctness}
supplies a pinned path, commit, extraction date, label, line range, and bounded
summary for each of the ten imported labels, and its proof states that no later
use may exceed that bounded summary.  Therefore a claim using only the lemma has
exactly the manual path-verified bounded-paraphrase evidence listed there.

Proposition~\ref{prop:source-interface-record-file-consistency} adds a different
finite record: the verifier parses the manuscript table, the JSON mirror, the
manifest's pinned-source-snapshot record, and the bundled source snapshot, and it
checks the six finite conditions enumerated in its proof.  Those checks upgrade
the source-interface premise only with respect to record-file consistency and
range containment.  The same proposition expressly excludes semantic truth of
the imported theorems and preserves the bounded-paraphrase restriction.  No row
in Table~\ref{tab:source-interface-record}, no field of
\path{source_interface_record.json}, and no command-boundary row records a fresh
Lean/BEDC rebuild or a semantic source-theorem verifier.  Hence an imported-label
premise has exactly the two evidence levels stated in the proposition and no
stronger one.

The finite-record interface theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface}, requires a discovery-gate source
interface with recorded evidence surface and boundary.  Applying the preceding
paragraphs to each of its imported discovery-gate citations gives precisely the
manual path-verified interface, optionally strengthened by the finite executable
record comparison, and forbids promotion of that interface into an unrecorded
semantic or rebuild claim.\end{proof}

\section{Operational interface}

\paragraph{Reader map.}
The supplement separates one central theorem chain from support-boundary audit
records.  The core finite-record safety argument is:
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface} fixes the certificate tuple,
claim kinds, gate dispatch, verifier predicate, evidence levels, and
record-gate-soundness hypothesis;
Definition~\ref{def:record-gate-soundness-external-interface} isolates that
hypothesis as an external finite input/output interface, and
Proposition~\ref{prop:record-gate-soundness-external-interface-exactness} proves
that it has no hidden semantic or venue-acceptance content;
Definition~\ref{def:certificate-schema-acceptance-table} restates the finite
acceptance predicates as the table relation \(\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}\);
Theorems~\ref{thm:verifier-input-output-contract},
\ref{thm:finite-verifier-normal-form},
\ref{thm:record-acceptance-exactness}, and
\ref{thm:finite-coordinate-determination-boundary} prove verifier exactness and
non-escalation from those predicates;
Theorem~\ref{thm:record-interface-rigidity} gives the record-interface rigidity
and fixed-point refresh criterion that turns these finite projections into a
typed interface specification rather than a count of unpacking lemmas;
Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} constructs finite publication
certificates under record-gate soundness; and
Theorem~\ref{thm:current-package-certificate-exactness} specializes the calculus
to the current six-row package.  The later results about packaging, upload
conditions, digests, command runs, inventories, venue records, and case snapshots
are deliberately theoremized audit-record consequences of finite rows and tables.
They document the support surface and its negative boundary; they should not be
read as independent mathematical invariants or as substitutes for the printed
TeX proofs in the core chain.

\subsection{Abstract finite-record interface}

For this long technical supplement and its compact CICM presentation artifact,
the following finite interface is the self-contained formal block used by every
later safety theorem.  It fixes, before use, the certificate tuple
\(\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)\), the dispatch table \(\Gamma\), the finite
verifier predicate \(V\), the acceptance relation \(\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}\), the
record-gate-soundness predicate \(\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)\), and the
stronger-reading preorder \(\preceq_{\Gamma}\).  All hypotheses in the headline
safety theorem are finite-record hypotheses over these objects; none is supplied
by a hidden semantic oracle, by the manual theorem inventory, or by generated
prose.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{p{0.27\linewidth}X}
\toprule
Term & Reviewer-facing meaning \\
\midrule
Record-gate soundness & Each accepted claim has the gate rows, evidence pointers,
evidence level, and promotion boundary assigned by \(\Gamma\); this is a finite
record predicate, not a proof that gate programs are correct \\
Finite certificate & The tuple \(\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)\) read by the
schema verifier for one claim: kind, level, evidence surface, human-promotion
field, gate rows, discovery rows, and command boundary \\
Finite bad subrecord & An inclusion-minimal subset of certificate fields whose
absence or mismatch causes the first schema rejection; every negative result below
points to such a missing coordinate \\
Stronger reading & A claim \(c^{+}\) with all coordinates of \(c\) plus an added
axis, evidence level, implementation, semantic, venue, support, theorem-ledger, or
command-run coordinate \\
Support coordinate & A finite upload, archive-equivalence, digest-binding,
source-state, command-log, or inventory field that must be present before local
support can be read externally \\
No-free-upgrade & A stronger reading is accepted exactly when its added finite
coordinate is supplied and passes the assigned gate; prose, inventory shape, or
local digest rows alone do not upgrade the claim \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\begin{definition}[Operational acceptance interface]
\label{def:operational-acceptance-interface}
A \emph{claim} is a manuscript assertion that can affect a mathematical,
artifact, route, or submission decision.  A \emph{load-bearing claim} is a claim
whose removal would change a theorem statement, a case-study conclusion, or the
submission-readiness status.  An \emph{advisory output} is any AI-agent draft,
score, suggested theorem, review packet, or repair proposal before a gate records
it.  A \emph{deterministic gate} is a repeatable predicate, script, or checklist
whose inputs and pass/fail decision are recorded independently of the prose
generated by an agent.  A \emph{human promotion} is the explicit editorial act
that moves a candidate into publication state, for example by creating an active
\texttt{2026\_*} paper directory with \texttt{main.tex} and \texttt{PIPELINE.md}.
An \emph{evidence surface} is the set of source paths, commits, commands, logs,
inventories, and witness records cited for a claim.  An \emph{acceptance entry}
is a manuscript or submission-ledger record that marks a candidate claim as
usable in the publication-facing argument.  \emph{Accepted work} is the subset of
candidate claims with such an entry.  This is a status notion only: the
definition records that an editorial acceptance entry exists, but it does not by
itself assert external editorial acceptance or implementation correctness.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{External hypothesis boundary.}
A pipeline is \emph{record-gate-sound for acceptance} when each acceptance entry records
the claim kind, the evidence surface, the evidence level, and a pass record for
every gate in $\Gamma$ assigned to that claim kind, and when a route-boundary
entry also records human promotion.  In this article that property is an
explicit finite predicate supplied as a hypothesis, written
$\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)$ below.  The definition does not prove that the
concrete scripts, daemons, checklists, or human processes generated the rows
truthfully; it only names the finite predicate that later conditional theorems
may assume.

The deterministic dispatch function $\Gamma$ from claim kinds to gates is part
of the operational interface.  Its domain is
\[
\{\text{formal-source},\text{ traceability},\text{ route},
\text{ submission},\text{ artifact},\text{ discovery},\text{ work-selection}\}.
\]
It sends formal-source claims to the build and axiom-purity gates; traceability
claims to inventory and marker-existence gates; route claims to promotion,
overlap, and submission-state gates; submission claims to submission-pack gates;
artifact claims to status and limitation-ledger gates; discovery claims to the
pinned discovery gate above and, for extension claims, to the theorem-content
delta gate; and work-selection claims to the scheduler gate, whose evidence
surface is a critical-path score or backlog window together with the claim kind
that the selected item is meant to advance.  For mixed claims, $\Gamma$ returns
the union of the gate sets for the claim kinds present.

The route gates have separate operational meanings.  The \emph{promotion gate}
uses the active-paper evidence surface, namely a human promotion act producing a
\path{2026_*} directory with \path{main.tex} and \path{PIPELINE.md}; passing
means the candidate may be daemon-visible publication work, and failing means it
remains intake or source material.  The \emph{overlap gate} uses route identity,
semantic-overlap ledgers, submitted-sibling paths, and program-board state;
passing means advancement is route-disjoint or has a recorded resolution, and
failing means advancement is blocked until closure, merge, supersession, or
waiting for prior feedback.  The \emph{submission-state gate} uses submission
markers, venue state, board state, and submission-pack metadata; passing means
the route's publication state permits the proposed action, and failing means the
action would duplicate, race, or under-specify an active or submitted route.  The
\emph{theorem-content delta gate} uses theorem inventories, hard-lint output, and
delta records such as \path{ARTIFACT_INVENTORY.md}; passing means that an
extension claim identifies load-bearing mathematical content, and failing means
that compilation, file churn, or surface edits may not be reported as substantive
theorem growth.

A \emph{reviewable artifact} for this paper is either a public repository file,
a supplemental file included with the submission, or an explicit
historical-evidence boundary stating that the local path is used only as
path-verified evidence and not as a fresh command-run claim.  A \emph{case
witness record} is path-complete when its evidence surface gives a
concrete source or artifact path for each load-bearing component of the row.  A
route-overlap witness has the fields \emph{route identity}, \emph{submitted
sibling}, \emph{overlap reason}, \emph{gate decision}, and \emph{allowed next
actions}.  An artifact-limitation witness has the fields \emph{artifact status
path}, \emph{limitation ledger path}, \emph{observed limitation}, \emph{gate
decision}, and \emph{allowed manuscript claim}.  A promotion witness has the
fields \emph{candidate surface}, \emph{human promotion evidence},
\emph{active-paper markers}, \emph{gate decision}, and \emph{allowed manuscript
claim}.  A theorem-content witness has the fields \emph{changed surface},
\emph{theorem inventory or hard-lint surface}, \emph{substantive-content delta},
\emph{gate decision}, and \emph{allowed manuscript claim}.  The inventory files
\path{ARTIFACT_INVENTORY.md}, \path{SOURCE_MAP.md}, and
\path{review_bundle/REVIEW_BUNDLE_MANIFEST.json} are part of the evidence surface
for this paper and give the compact path catalogue used by
Table~\ref{tab:case-witnesses}.

The same interface can be read without the local route vocabulary.  A
\emph{portable workflow schema} is the seven-sorted finite record
\[
\mathcal{S}=(\mathsf{Claim},\mathsf{Kind},\mathsf{Surface},\mathsf{Gate},
\mathsf{Pass},\mathsf{Prom},\mathsf{Level})
\]
together with predicates
\[
\operatorname{typed}(c,k),\quad
\operatorname{surface}(c,E),\quad
\operatorname{assigned}(k,g),\quad
\operatorname{passes}(p,g,E,\ell),\quad
\operatorname{promoted}(c,h),
\]
and a boundary predicate \(\operatorname{bounded}(c,\ell,B)\).  The local names in
this paper instantiate these sorts as follows: manuscript assertions are in
\(\mathsf{Claim}\); the domain of \(\Gamma\) is \(\mathsf{Kind}\); paths,
commits, manifests, inventories, snapshots, and logs are elements of
\(\mathsf{Surface}\); the rows of Table~\ref{tab:gates} are elements of
\(\mathsf{Gate}\); tuples \(\rho=(g,I,d,e,\ell)\) are elements of
\(\mathsf{Pass}\); intake-to-active-paper moves are elements of
\(\mathsf{Prom}\); and \(\{\text{path-verified},\text{command-run}\}\subset
\mathsf{Level}\).  A local path, route state, or daemon marker is portable only
through the corresponding element of \(\mathsf{Surface}\), \(\mathsf{Gate}\),
\(\mathsf{Pass}\), or \(\mathsf{Prom}\); the concrete spelling of the path or
route name is not part of the portable claim.

The six venue-independent roles carried by this schema are the following.  The
\emph{source object} is the structured mathematical object, artifact family, or
publication route state affected by a claim.  The \emph{formal interface} is the
typed boundary through which selected source-object assertions are represented
for Lean, a script verifier, a manifest checker, or another mechanical checker.
The \emph{finite evidence row} is a bounded path, manifest, command, marker,
log, digest, or limitation row submitted for that interface.  The
\emph{advisory agent action} is a proposal, repair, ranking, or review item before
it is accepted by a gate.  The \emph{deterministic gate} is the finite predicate
assigned to the claim kind.  The \emph{human promotion boundary} is the editorial
act that moves accepted material from intake or source work into the public
manuscript state.  Local artifacts such as \path{main.tex}, Lean markers,
review-bundle JSON files, route labels, and stage logs are examples of these
roles, not primitives of the method.

\begin{theorem}[Support: portable six-role finite-record factorization]
\label{thm:portable-six-role-interface}
Let \(P\) be a package satisfying
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}.  For each load-bearing
claim \(c\) accepted by \(P\), there is a finite six-role record
\[
\Pi(c)=(S_c,F_c,W_c,A_c,G_c,M_c)
\]
with the following interpretation: \(S_c\) is the source object, \(F_c\) is the
formal interface, \(W_c\) is the finite evidence row surface, \(A_c\) is the set
of advisory agent actions associated with the candidate, \(G_c\) is the finite
set of deterministic gate pass records assigned to the claim kind, and \(M_c\)
is either the human-promotion record or the marker that no promotion boundary is
crossed.  Acceptance of \(c\) depends on the local artifact names only through
\(\Pi(c)\) and the evidence level \(\ell\).  More precisely, if another workflow
\(P'\) preserves the six roles by maps
\[
S_c\mapsto S'_c,
\quad F_c\mapsto F'_c,
\quad W_c\mapsto W'_c,
\quad A_c\mapsto A'_c,
\quad G_c\mapsto G'_c,
\quad M_c\mapsto M'_c
\]
so that claim kinds, assigned gates, pass/fail decisions, evidence levels, and
promotion-boundary status are preserved, then \(P'\) has the same finite-record
accepted reading for \(c\).  Conversely, any accepted reading of \(c\) in this
paper determines such a six-role record.  No implementation-soundness,
proof-assistant-soundness, dynamic artifact-validity, external-upload, or
venue-acceptance claim is invariant under this transfer unless it is represented
as an additional source object or formal interface together with its own finite
evidence row, deterministic gate, and promotion boundary.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Start with an accepted load-bearing claim \(c\) and its publication certificate
\(\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)\).  The source object \(S_c\) is the finite
component of the evidence surface named by the claim: for example a structured
definition/theorem surface, a manifest-bounded artifact family, or a route-state
surface.  The formal interface \(F_c\) is the finite typed boundary selected by
the claim kinds in \(K\): the build or marker interface for formal-source and
traceability claims, the manifest/evaluator interface for artifact claims, the
route-state interface for route and submission claims, and the theorem-content or
discovery interface for discovery and work-selection claims.  The finite
evidence row surface \(W_c\) is the corresponding finite subset of \(E\) together
with the boundary field \(B\).  The advisory-action component \(A_c\) is the
finite set of submitted proposal, review, repair, ranking, or discovery rows
associated with the candidate; if no such rows are submitted, it is empty.  The
deterministic-gate component \(G_c\) is exactly the finite set \(R\) of pass
records for \(\bigcup_{k\in K}\Gamma(k)\).  The promotion component \(M_c\) is
\(H\).  Hence \(\Pi(c)\) is finite and is constructed entirely from the certificate
fields required by Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}.

The certificate verifier and the acceptance predicate inspect only claim kind,
evidence level, evidence surface membership, assigned gates, pass records,
discovery rows when present, and the promotion/boundary fields.  They do not
inspect the semantic spelling of a directory name, route label, script filename,
or local stage number except as an element of those finite fields.  Therefore a
