workflow \(P'\) that preserves the six roles, the claim kinds, the gate
assignment relation, the pass/fail decisions, the evidence level, and the
promotion-boundary status can reconstruct a certificate
\(\mathcal C'(c)=(K,\ell,E',H',R',D',B')\) satisfying the same acceptance clauses:
\(E'\) is supplied by \(W'_c\), \(R'\) by \(G'_c\), \(H'\) by \(M'_c\), and the
interface/discovery/boundary fields by \(F'_c\), \(A'_c\), and \(W'_c\).  Thus the
finite-record accepted reading is preserved.

Conversely, any accepted reading in this paper already has the certificate
\(\mathcal C(c)\).  Applying the construction in the first paragraph gives the
six-role record, so no accepted local reading can depend on a path name, route
label, or package-byte state without first passing through one of the six roles.
The final sentence follows from the same finite-coordinate argument used by the
operational interface: each stronger reading names an additional axis not read by
\(\Pi(c)\).  Without adding that axis as a new role component with its evidence
row and assigned gate, two workflows can agree on \(\Pi(c)\) while disagreeing on
the stronger fact.  Hence such a stronger fact is not invariant under the
portable transfer.\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Portable workflow-schema factorisation]
\label{prop:portable-workflow-schema-factorisation}
Let \(P\) be any package satisfying
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}, and let
\(c\) be a load-bearing claim accepted by \(P\) with certificate
\(\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)\).  Under the six-role interface of
Theorem~\ref{thm:portable-six-role-interface} and the map from the local automath
and newmath artifacts to the seven sorts of \(\mathcal{S}\) just defined, acceptance
of \(c\) factors through the following venue-independent predicate:
\[
\operatorname{Accept}_{\mathcal{S}}(c) \Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl[\forall k\in K\,\operatorname{typed}(c,k)\Bigr]
\wedge \operatorname{surface}(c,E)
\wedge \Bigl[\forall k\in K\,\forall g\,(
\operatorname{assigned}(k,g)\Rightarrow
\exists p\in R\,\operatorname{passes}(p,g,E,\ell))\Bigr]
\wedge \operatorname{bounded}(c,\ell,B)
\]
with the additional conjunct \(\operatorname{promoted}(c,H)\) exactly when the
claim crosses an intake-to-publication boundary.  Consequently replacing local
paths, route directories, or tool names by another venue's surfaces and gates
preserves the accepted finite-record reading whenever the seven sorted fields and
the displayed predicate are preserved.  It does not preserve, and therefore does
not assert, implementation soundness, proof-assistant soundness, fresh dynamic
artifact validity, external upload, or venue acceptance unless those stronger
coordinates are supplied as additional sorted fields and pass records.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}, an accepted
load-bearing claim has a nonempty finite set \(K\) of claim kinds, an evidence
surface \(E\), a level \(\ell\), one pass record in \(R\) for each gate assigned
by \(\Gamma\) to a kind in \(K\), a human-promotion field \(H\) when the route
boundary is crossed, and a boundary field \(B\) distinguishing path-verified from
command-run support.  The displayed schema map sends exactly those components to
\(\mathsf{Kind}\), \(\mathsf{Surface}\), \(\mathsf{Level}\), \(\mathsf{Gate}\),
\(\mathsf{Pass}\), \(\mathsf{Prom}\), and the boundary predicate.  Thus every
local acceptance entry satisfies the displayed predicate: \(\operatorname{typed}\)
records membership in \(K\), \(\operatorname{surface}\) records \(E\),
\(\operatorname{assigned}\) is the graph of \(\Gamma\),
\(\operatorname{passes}\) is witnessed by the required pass rows in \(R\),
\(\operatorname{promoted}\) is witnessed by \(H\) in the route-boundary cases,
and \(\operatorname{bounded}\) is witnessed by \(B\).

Conversely, suppose the seven sorted fields and the displayed predicate are
preserved after replacing the concrete local artifacts by another venue's
surfaces and gates.  For each accepted kind the predicate supplies every assigned
gate and a pass record at the declared level, and it supplies the promotion
record exactly in the boundary-crossing cases.  Reassembling those witnesses as
\((K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)\) gives the finite certificate required by the operational
acceptance interface.  The reassembly uses only typed fields and finite pass
records, not the names of local directories or daemons.  Finally, the last
sentence follows from the boundary field \(B\) and the no-free-upgrade part of
the interface: stronger readings require extra coordinates and assigned pass
records, so they cannot be reconstructed from preservation of the seven fields
alone.\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Finite-record projection preorder]
\label{def:finite-record-projection-preorder}
Fix a finite coordinate universe \(U\) consisting of the fields named by the
portable schema, the dispatch table \(\Gamma\), and any explicitly declared
extension coordinates.  A \emph{finite record} is a pair \(r=(D_r,v_r)\), where
\(D_r\subseteq U\) is finite and \(v_r\) assigns one value to every coordinate in
\(D_r\).  For two finite records write \(r\leq_U r'\) when
\(D_r\subseteq D_{r'}\) and \(v_{r'}|_{D_r}=v_r\).  A claim reading \(c^{+}\) is a
\emph{proper stronger reading} of \(c\), written
\(c\prec_{\Gamma,U}c^{+}\), when the accepted certificate record of \(c\) is
\(\leq_U\) the certificate record required by \(c^{+}\), and the latter has at
least one extra coordinate assigned by \(\Gamma\) or by a declared extension gate.
The older notation \(c\preceq_{\Gamma}c^{+}\) is used below only for this
schema-relative preorder.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Finite-record normal-form and missing-coordinate uniqueness]
\label{lem:finite-record-preorder-normal-form}
In the finite-record projection preorder of
Definition~\ref{def:finite-record-projection-preorder}:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(\leq_U\) is a partial order on finite records.
\item If \(r\leq_U r'\), then the projection of \(r'\) to \(D_r\) is uniquely
\(r\).
\item If a stronger reading requires a coordinate set \(D^{+}\) and the available
record has coordinate set \(D\subset D^{+}\) with strict inclusion, then the first missing coordinate
in any fixed printed order of \(U\), together with the stronger-reading tag, is an
inclusion-minimal finite bad subrecord for the attempted upgrade.
\item If finite records \(r_1,\ldots,r_n\) have domains contained in
\(D\subseteq U\), then their finite conjunction has domain contained in \(D\).  In
particular, no conjunction of bounded support rows determines a coordinate in
\(U\setminus D\).
\end{enumerate}
All four assertions are schema-relative: changing \(U\), the printed coordinate
order, or the dispatch table is a new finite-record problem, not a consequence of
this lemma.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Reflexivity of \(\leq_U\) is immediate.  Transitivity follows because if
\(D_r\subseteq D_{r'}\subseteq D_{r''}\) and the two restriction equalities hold,
then \(v_{r''}|_{D_r}=v_r\).  Antisymmetry follows because \(D_r=D_{r'}\) and the
two value functions agree on that common domain.  Thus \(\leq_U\) is a partial
order.  The second assertion is the definition of restriction: a function on
\(D_{r'}\) has only one restriction to the subset \(D_r\).

For the third assertion, choose the least coordinate
\(u\in D^{+}\setminus D\) in the fixed printed order.  The available record has no
value for \(u\), so any verifier whose schema requires \(u\) for the stronger
reading must reject before accepting that reading.  The pair consisting of the
stronger-reading tag and \(u\) is finite.  Removing the tag leaves no request for
the stronger reading; removing \(u\) leaves the available record unchanged on all
coordinates it contains and therefore cannot exhibit the first absent required
coordinate.  Hence the bad subrecord is inclusion-minimal for this schema and
order.  Finally, the conjunction of finitely many records is obtained by taking
the union of their finite domains and requiring agreement on overlaps.  If every
domain is contained in \(D\), so is the union.  Therefore a coordinate outside
\(D\) cannot be recovered from such a conjunction.\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Portable method normal form and local-support pullback]
\label{prop:portable-method-normal-form-local-pullback}
Let \(P\) be a package satisfying
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}.  Every load-bearing
accepted claim \(c\) in \(P\) admits a unique weakest portable method normal form,
up to isomorphism of finite records in the schema-relative preorder of
Definition~\ref{def:finite-record-projection-preorder},
\[
\mathsf{NF}(c)=(S_c,F_c,W_c,A_c,G_c,M_c,\ell_c,B_c),
\]
where \((S_c,F_c,W_c,A_c,G_c,M_c)\) is the six-role record of
Theorem~\ref{thm:portable-six-role-interface}, \(\ell_c\) is the declared evidence
level, and \(B_c\) is the boundary field distinguishing local path-verified,
historical, command-run, external-support, formal-source, and artifact-semantic
coordinates.  A local support statement using paths, route labels, round names,
package bytes, inventory files, digest rows, or case-snapshot files is accepted by
the portable method exactly when it is the pullback of such a normal form along
the evident map from local names to the eight displayed fields.  Consequently a
local path, digest, stage label, or package fixed point can never be a primitive
certificate of the method: it contributes only through \(W_c\), \(G_c\), \(B_c\),
or \(M_c\).  In particular, absence of the upload/archive, fresh formal-source
rebuild, or dynamic artifact-evaluator coordinate in \(B_c\) forces the accepted
reading to remain respectively local/path-verified, source-interface bounded, or
manifest/historical.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:portable-six-role-interface} constructs the finite six-role
record \(\Pi(c)=(S_c,F_c,W_c,A_c,G_c,M_c)\) from the certificate
\(\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)\).  Adjoin to \(\Pi(c)\) the two certificate
fields that determine the strength of the reading, namely the evidence level
\(\ell\) and the boundary field \(B\).  This gives the displayed tuple
\(\mathsf{NF}(c)\).  Regard it as a finite record whose coordinate domain is the
eight displayed fields inside the universe of
Definition~\ref{def:finite-record-projection-preorder}.  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-record-preorder-normal-form}, projection to this domain is
unique; hence the normal form is unique up to coordinate-preserving renaming.
It is weakest because deleting any one of its components identifies two
certificate states that the operational interface is allowed to distinguish:
deleting \(S_c\) forgets the source object; deleting \(F_c\) forgets
which formal interface is being checked; deleting \(W_c\) forgets the submitted
finite evidence; deleting \(A_c\) forgets whether an agent action is merely
advisory or has been submitted for gate treatment; deleting \(G_c\) forgets the
deterministic pass records; deleting \(M_c\) forgets whether a human promotion
boundary was crossed; deleting \(\ell\) collapses path-verified and command-run
readings; and deleting \(B\) collapses local, external, formal-source, and
artifact-semantic coordinates.  Each collapse changes at least one acceptance or
non-escalation clause in Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface},
so no smaller tuple is sufficient for all load-bearing claims.

Now consider a local support statement.  Its concrete names---for example
\path{main.tex}, \path{theorem_inventory.json}, a route directory, a stage label,
\path{review_bundle/FINAL_DIGESTS_SHA256.md}, or a case-snapshot file---enter the
operational interface only as source objects, finite evidence rows, pass records,
boundary fields, or promotion records.  Mapping each such local name to the
corresponding component of \(\mathsf{NF}(c)\) is therefore a pullback of the
portable predicate of Proposition~\ref{prop:portable-workflow-schema-factorisation}.
If the pullback supplies the assigned gates and declared level, the claim is
accepted at that finite-record level; if it omits a required coordinate, the
missing component is an inclusion-minimal bad subrecord by
Proposition~\ref{prop:publication-safety-minimal-bad-record-witness}.  Thus local
names have no independent certifying force outside the normal form.

The final sentence is an immediate application of the boundary component.  The
positive external-support reading requires the upload or archive-equivalence
fields classified in Corollary~\ref{cor:upload-or-archive-instantiation-record};
the fresh formal-source reading requires the rebuild and axiom-audit fields
separated in Theorem~\ref{thm:source-interface-semantic-completeness-obstruction};
and the artifact-semantic reading requires the evaluator and rerun fields isolated
by Corollary~\ref{cor:artifact-semantic-validity-boundary}.  When \(B_c\) lacks one
of those coordinates, Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-coordinate-determination-boundary}
prevents reconstruction of that stronger coordinate from paths, digest rows,
round labels, or package bytes.  The accepted reading is therefore exactly the
weaker local/path-verified, bounded source-interface, or manifest/historical
reading stated in the proposition.\end{proof}

We distinguish two evidence levels.  A claim is \emph{path-verified} when this
paper records the relevant source path, artifact path, pinned commit or local
publication path, and gate decision, but does not assert that a command was
freshly rerun for this submission.  A claim is \emph{command-run} when the paper
also records the command, source commit, environment, exit code, and log path
for a fresh run.  This long technical supplement uses path-verified architecture
and case evidence unless explicitly marked command-run.

A uniform \emph{pass record} is the finite tuple
\[
\rho=(g,I,d,e,\ell),
\]
where $g$ is the gate name, $I$ is the input surface submitted to that gate,
$d$ is the recorded decision, $e$ is the evidence pointer supporting the
decision, and $\ell$ is the evidence level.  A pass record is assigned to a
claim certificate only when its evidence pointer is contained in the claim's
evidence surface, in a submitted manifest or table row, in a bundled snapshot, or
in an explicit historical-evidence boundary.

A \emph{publication certificate} for a load-bearing claim $c$ is the finite
record
\[
\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B).
\]
Here $K$ is the nonempty finite set of claim kinds carried by $c$, $\ell$ is the
evidence level, $E$ is the evidence surface, $H$ is either a human-promotion
record or the marker that $c$ does not cross the intake-to-publication boundary,
$R$ gives one pass record, with the five fields above, for each gate in
$\bigcup_{k\in K}\Gamma(k)$, $D$ is present exactly when $K$ contains discovery
and then names the pinned discovery-gate source-interface rows used for the
claim, and $B$ records either the command-run fields or the explicit boundary
that no command-run assertion is made.  A certificate is \emph{locally
checkable} when these finite fields are present and every path, manifest row, or
log named by a field lies in the submitted artifact, the supplemental review
bundle, or the explicit path-verified historical boundary.

For later use we make the local check explicit as a finite verifier.  The
concrete package checker supplied with the review bundle is
\path{review_bundle/verify_certificate_records.py}.  Its positive invocation is
\path{python review_bundle/verify_certificate_records.py}; it reads exactly
\path{review_bundle/certificate_schema.json},
\path{review_bundle/current_package_pass_records.json},
\path{review_bundle/submission_interface_map.json},
\path{review_bundle/primary_claim_inventory.json}, and
\path{review_bundle/REVIEW_BUNDLE_MANIFEST.json}, and writes the recorded pass log
\path{review_bundle/certificate_verification_run.log}.  Its negative-example
invocation is
\path{python review_bundle/verify_certificate_records.py --negative-example review_bundle/negative_certificate_record_example.json},
with recorded log \path{review_bundle/negative_certificate_record_example_run.md};
that fixture upgrades a route row to command-run strength while omitting the
command-run tuple and is rejected with the finite bad subrecord
\path{neg1: command-run fields incomplete}.  The mathematical verifier below is
the schema abstraction of this package checker.

Let \(\mathsf{Dom}(\Gamma)\) be the seven-kind domain and let
\(\mathsf{Lev}=\{\mathsf{path},\mathsf{command}\}\).  For a candidate record
\(\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)\), define six finite predicates:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[$P_1$:] $K\ne\emptyset$, $K\subseteq\mathsf{Dom}(\Gamma)$, and
$\ell\in\mathsf{Lev}$.
\item[$P_2$:] $E$ is finite and each item of $E$ is a submitted path,
review-bundle path, manifest row, log path, pinned commit, or explicit
historical-evidence boundary.
\item[$P_3$:] for every gate $g\in\bigcup_{k\in K}\Gamma(k)$, $R$ contains a
pass record $(g,I,d,e,\ell')$ whose evidence pointer lies in $E$ or in a named
submitted table, manifest row, bundled snapshot, or historical boundary.
\item[$P_4$:] $H$ records the human promotion exactly when $c$ crosses the
intake-to-publication boundary and otherwise records that no such boundary is
crossed.
\item[$P_5$:] $D$ is present exactly when discovery lies in $K$, and then names
the pinned discovery-gate source-interface rows used by the claim.
\item[$P_6$:] $B$ either records command, source commit, environment, exit code,
and log path for command-run evidence or explicitly records that no command-run
assertion is made.
\end{enumerate}
Define the finite verifier
\[
V(c,\mathcal C)=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{6}P_i(c,\mathcal C,\Gamma).
\]
If this conjunction is false, the rejected subrecord is the finite set of fields
read by the least-indexed failed predicate.  This paragraph defines the verifier
only; no unprinted semantic oracle is part of it.  The next definition packages
the same finite fields as an explicit input type and a finite acceptance table;
the exactness theorem below then proves that the verifier and the independently
named record-acceptance relation coincide on that finite data structure.

For a package $P$ with ledger $L$, dispatch table $\Gamma$, and submitted
support surface $S$, write
\[
\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)
\]
for the following finite predicate.  For every acceptance entry of a
load-bearing claim $c$ in $L$, there is a publication certificate
$\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)$ such that $E\subseteq S$, $V(c,\mathcal C)=1$,
each pass record in $R$ is a submitted row of $L$, the row decision is passing,
and the row's evidence pointer denotes an element of $S$ at the evidence level
recorded in the row.  If $B$ does not contain command, source state,
environment, exit code, and log path, then $\mathsf{RGS}_{S}$ asserts only this
finite row-and-pointer property and asserts no implementation-level correctness
of the gate that produced the row.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Record-gate soundness external interface]
\label{def:record-gate-soundness-external-interface}
The external record-gate interface for a package is the finite predicate
\[
\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)
\]
with the following inputs and outputs.  Its inputs are exactly a package $P$, a
submitted support surface $S$, a finite acceptance ledger $L$, and the deterministic
claim-kind dispatch table $\Gamma$ of
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}.  Its positive output is the
finite family of certificates
\[
\{\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B): c\in L
\text{ is an accepted load-bearing claim}\}
\]
such that $E\subseteq S$, $V(c,\mathcal C(c))=1$, every assigned gate in
$\bigcup_{k\in K}\Gamma(k)$ has a submitted passing row in $R$, each evidence
pointer in such a row denotes an element of $S$ at the recorded evidence level,
the human-promotion coordinate $H$ is present exactly at an intake-to-publication
crossing, and the discovery and command-boundary coordinates $D$ and $B$ have the
presence conditions required by the verifier predicates $P_5$ and $P_6$.  Its
negative output, when the predicate fails for a ledger row, is only the finite bad
subrecord read by the first failed verifier predicate among $P_1,\ldots,P_6$.

This interface is an accepted-row hypothesis, not a theorem generated by the
pipeline itself.  This interface makes no further claim.  In particular it does not assert that an
external venue accepted the work, that a command was freshly rerun, that a Lean
development builds, that an artifact has the semantic property named in prose, or
that an advisory agent output is proof evidence, unless the corresponding source
path, command, source state, environment, exit code, log path, or gate row is one
of the finite coordinates read above.  Consequently every later
publication-safety theorem using this interface must display
\(\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)\), or an accepted row asserting that predicate for
the same package, as a hypothesis.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Conditional record-gate interface equivalence and non-claim boundary]
\label{prop:record-gate-soundness-external-interface-exactness}
For the operational acceptance interface of
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}, the standalone interface in
Definition~\ref{def:record-gate-soundness-external-interface} is equivalent to the
predicate $\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)$ used in the publication-safety theorem.
Moreover, conditional on an accepted instance of this interface, every consequence used by
Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} is determined by the finite
coordinates $(P,S,L,\Gamma)$ and by the displayed certificates
$\mathcal C(c)$; no implementation-level, semantic, venue-acceptance,
fresh-execution, or advisory-evidence claim follows from record-gate soundness
unless it appears as one of those finite coordinates.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The predicate $\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)$ in
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface} quantifies over exactly the
accepted load-bearing ledger entries $c\in L$ and requires exactly the following
data: a certificate $\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)$, containment $E\subseteq S$,
acceptance by the finite verifier $V$, submitted passing rows for the pass records
in $R$, and evidence pointers denoting elements of $S$ at the recorded evidence
levels.  The verifier definition expands $V(c,\mathcal C(c))=1$ into the six
predicates $P_1,\ldots,P_6$, which are precisely the kind, evidence-surface,
assigned-gate, human-promotion, discovery, and command-boundary presence
conditions listed in
Definition~\ref{def:record-gate-soundness-external-interface}.  Hence a positive
instance of one definition supplies a positive instance of the other, with the
same certificates and the same submitted rows; conversely the standalone
interface supplies every finite field required by the original predicate, so the
original predicate holds.

For the boundary statement, inspect the fields read by $P_1,\ldots,P_6$.  They
contain claim kinds, evidence levels, finite evidence pointers, human-promotion
markers, assigned gate rows, discovery rows, and the command-run or no-command-run
boundary.  None of these fields is a venue decision, a proof-assistant semantic
judgment, an artifact semantic evaluator, a live daemon state, or an advisory
agent proof object unless an additional row explicitly records that fact as an
evidence coordinate satisfying the same verifier predicates.  Therefore the
interface can be used in Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} only to
construct finite publication certificates and finite bad subrecords.  Any stronger
reading would require an added coordinate and is outside the predicate just proved
equivalent.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Support: accepted-RGS conditional compact-spine normal form]
\label{thm:rgs-conditional-compact-spine}
Fix a presentation-only package with submitted surface $S$, acceptance ledger
$L$, dispatch table $\Gamma$, and finite verifier $V$ as in
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}.  Suppose the compact
article cites the reviewer-facing spine
\[
\text{Theorems~\ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface} and
\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface}, and Corollary~
\ref{cor:primary-presentation-weak-interface-compression}.}
\]
Then every load-bearing publication-safety sentence supported by that spine has
the accepted-RGS conditional finite-record normal form:
\[
\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl(\mathsf{Out}_{\Gamma,S}(L),\mathsf{Bad}_{\Gamma,S}(L),
\Pi_{\mathrm{pres}}(S,L,\Gamma)\bigr).
\]
Thus the compact paper may state conditional finite-record certificate safety,
schema-relative verifier exactness, and finite bad-subrecord maximality, but it
may not state end-to-end gate implementation soundness for the concrete gate
programs unless the support surface is enlarged by the gate-implementation
coordinates required by
Theorem~\ref{thm:gate-implementation-soundness-upgrade-obstruction} or by an
equivalent implementation-soundness extension coordinate accepted under the same
schema.  If a compact-paper sentence omits the record-gate-soundness premise but
keeps the finite-record publication-safety conclusion, or if it replaces the finite-record
conclusion by concrete gate implementation soundness, then its first missing
field is respectively the $\mathsf{RGS}$ premise or the gate-implementation
extension coordinate, and that missing field together with the stronger-reading
tag is an inclusion-minimal bad subrecord.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:record-gate-soundness-external-interface-exactness},
the predicate $\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)$ is exactly the external finite
row-and-pointer interface available to the publication-safety theorem.  Its
positive data are the certificates $\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)$ satisfying
the six verifier predicates, and its negative data are only the finite bad
subrecords read by the first failed predicate.  Therefore any safety conclusion
that uses this interface and no additional support field is a function only of
the finite submitted surface, ledger, dispatch table, verifier predicates, and
certificates.

Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} identifies that function: from
the same inputs and under $\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)$ it constructs
$\mathsf{Out}_{\Gamma,S}(L)$ and the rejected bad-subrecord list, and it proves
schema-relative exactness for the accepted certificate records.  Theorem
\ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface} then projects exactly these data,
together with the axis map and boundary list, to
$\Pi_{\mathrm{pres}}(S,L,\Gamma)$.  Hence a compact citation of the spine has the
displayed normal form: the premise is the record-gate-soundness predicate, and
the conclusion is the finite accepted-certificate/bad-subrecord/presentation
projection.  No smaller formula can carry the same safety assertion, because
removing the premise leaves no hypothesis that supplies the passing gate rows
and evidence pointers, while removing the conclusion removes one of the finite
outputs actually constructed by the theorem chain.

It remains to classify the two overclaims named in the statement.  If the compact
sentence drops $\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)$ while retaining the
finite-record publication-safety conclusion, two package states can agree on all printed
presentation prose and differ only in whether the required ledger rows and
evidence pointers pass the predicate.  The verifier cannot accept the safety
conclusion in the failing state; the missing premise is therefore the first bad
subrecord.  If the sentence instead asserts concrete implementation soundness of
the gate programs, it changes the stronger-reading tag from finite row-and-pointer
soundness to implementation soundness.  The finite certificate fields do not read
gate source code, executable specifications, negative tests, reproducibility data,
or proof links tying program behavior to the record predicate.  Theorem
\ref{thm:gate-implementation-soundness-upgrade-obstruction} lists exactly the
finite coordinate families that must be added for that upgrade.  Without them,
Corollary~\ref{cor:primary-presentation-weak-interface-compression} classifies the stronger
tag together with the absent upgrade coordinate as an inclusion-minimal bad
subrecord; with them, the same schema accepts the enlarged claim.  Thus the
conditional finite-record wording is not a stylistic hedge but the unique compact
normal form of the reviewer-facing spine.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Current-package record-gate hypothesis boundary]
\label{thm:current-package-rgs-instantiation-boundary}
Let $P_{0}$ be the current CICM presentation-only package, let $S_{0}$ be the
local support surface of Proposition~\ref{prop:final-package-shape-convention},
let $L_{0}$ be the finite acceptance ledger used by the present theorem chain,
and let $\Gamma_{0}$ be the dispatch table of
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}.  The safety conclusions of
Theorems~\ref{thm:rgs-conditional-compact-spine},
\ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface}, and
\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} instantiate unconditionally for
$(P_{0},S_{0},L_{0},\Gamma_{0})$ if and only if the submitted finite record
contains an accepted record-gate-soundness row for exactly this package, surface,
ledger, and dispatch table.  Absent that row, the present source proves only
\[
\mathsf{RGS}_{S_{0}}(P_{0},L_{0},\Gamma_{0})
\Longrightarrow
\bigl(\mathsf{Out}_{\Gamma_{0},S_{0}}(L_{0}),
\mathsf{Bad}_{\Gamma_{0},S_{0}}(L_{0}),
\Pi_{\mathrm{pres}}(S_{0},L_{0},\Gamma_{0})\bigr),
\]
and the omitted record-gate-soundness row is the first missing coordinate of any
unconditional publication-safety reading.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose first that the submitted finite record contains an accepted
record-gate-soundness row for exactly $(P_{0},S_{0},L_{0},\Gamma_{0})$.  By
Definition~\ref{def:record-gate-soundness-external-interface}, such a row is
precisely a positive finite instance of
$\mathsf{RGS}_{S_{0}}(P_{0},L_{0},\Gamma_{0})$: for every accepted load-bearing
claim in $L_{0}$ it supplies the certificate
$\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)$, the containment $E\subseteq S_{0}$, passing
verifier status, submitted passing gate rows, and evidence pointers into
$S_{0}$.  Substituting this positive instance into
Theorem~\ref{thm:rgs-conditional-compact-spine} yields the displayed finite
certificate, bad-subrecord, and presentation-projection conclusion for the
current package.  Theorems~\ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface} and
\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} use no additional unrecorded semantic or
implementation premise, so this is exactly the unconditional instantiation they
can receive from the finite record.

Conversely, suppose the source is read as asserting the same publication-safety
conclusion for $(P_{0},S_{0},L_{0},\Gamma_{0})$ without an accepted
record-gate-soundness row.  The verifier has no finite field from which to infer,
for each accepted load-bearing row of $L_{0}$, both the required gate-pass rows
and the evidence-pointer membership assertions in $S_{0}$.  Two finite package
states may therefore agree on $P_{0}$, $S_{0}$, $L_{0}$, $\Gamma_{0}$, the printed
prose, and all non-RGS support rows, while differing only in the truth of the
missing RGS row.  In the state where the row is absent, predicate A3 of the
certificate schema, equivalently the corresponding conjunct of $V$, is not
supplied for the unconditional reading.  Proposition~\ref{prop:record-gate-soundness-external-interface-exactness}
then identifies the absent row as exactly the finite coordinate that separates
the conditional theorem from the unconditional reading.

Minimality follows because adding that single accepted row supplies the premise
of the conditional theorem, while deleting the stronger tag ``unconditional
workflow or venue publication safety'' leaves the conditional finite-record assertion already
proved above.  Thus the manuscript neither proves nor needs a workflow-level RGS
fact silently: it proves the conditional safety theorem, and it proves that the
unique finite upgrade to an unconditional current-package instantiation is an
accepted RGS row for the same package, ledger, surface, and dispatch table.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Current package has no implicit record-gate discharge]
\label{cor:current-package-no-implicit-rgs-discharge}
For the current tuple $(P_{0},S_{0},L_{0},\Gamma_{0})$ of
Theorem~\ref{thm:current-package-rgs-instantiation-boundary}, the finite support
records supplied by the theorem inventory, the theorem-environment extractor,
the retained certificate/source-interface/primary-claim verifiers, and the final
digest manifest do not by themselves instantiate
$\mathsf{RGS}_{S_{0}}(P_{0},L_{0},\Gamma_{0})$.  Hence the master presentation
interface in Theorems~\ref{thm:rgs-conditional-compact-spine},
\ref{thm:presentation-compressed-interface}, and
\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} remains conditional on
$\mathsf{RGS}_{S_{0}}(P_{0},L_{0},\Gamma_{0})$ unless the submitted finite record
contains an accepted record-gate-soundness row whose package, support surface,
ledger, and dispatch table are exactly $(P_{0},S_{0},L_{0},\Gamma_{0})$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Each listed support record has a syntactic or finite-record role fixed elsewhere
in the theorem chain: the inventory and extractor rows classify labelled
theorem-like environments, the retained verifier rows check the declared
certificate/source-interface/primary-claim schemas, and the digest manifest binds
bytes of those rows.  None of these coordinate types is the
record-gate-soundness row defined in
Definition~\ref{def:record-gate-soundness-external-interface}: they do not assert,
for every accepted row of $L_{0}$, the full conjunction of gate-pass rows,
evidence-pointer membership in $S_{0}$, and dispatch-table soundness for exactly
$(P_{0},S_{0},L_{0},\Gamma_{0})$.  By
Theorem~\ref{thm:current-package-rgs-instantiation-boundary}, that exact accepted
row is the necessary and sufficient finite coordinate for turning the conditional
current-package safety interface into an unconditional instance.  Its absence
therefore leaves precisely the displayed RGS hypothesis, and its presence is the
single finite-record discharge of that hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Stronger-reading preorder]
\label{def:stronger-reading-preorder}
Fix the dispatch table $\Gamma$ and certificate tuple
$\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)$ of
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}.  A proposed reading
$c^{+}$ of the same prose claim is \emph{record-stronger} than $c$, written
$c\preceq_{\Gamma} c^{+}$, if at least one of the following finite coordinates is
strictly enlarged while the others are unchanged or enlarged: the claim-kind set
$K$; the evidence level, from $\mathsf{path}$ to $\mathsf{command}$; the evidence
surface $E$; the promotion field $H$; the assigned gate-pass family $R$; the
discovery-interface field $D$; or the boundary field $B$.  It is
\emph{properly stronger} if the enlargement is strict in at least one coordinate.
It is \emph{accepted as a stronger reading} only when the enlarged tuple still
satisfies $\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}$: every newly added kind has its assigned gates,
every newly raised evidence level has the command tuple required by A6, and every
new evidence item is on the submitted support surface or in an explicit
historical boundary.

This is the certificate-tuple specialization of the finite-record projection
preorder of Definition~\ref{def:finite-record-projection-preorder}, with
coordinate universe
\(U=\{K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B\}\) enlarged by any declared extension gates.  The preorder
is intentionally syntactic and finite-record based.  It is not a semantic
entailment relation between mathematical propositions, and it does not turn an
inventory entry, digest row, or path reference into proof evidence for a
theorem-like environment.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Certificate-schema acceptance table]
\label{def:certificate-schema-acceptance-table}
Fix the seven-kind dispatch table $\Gamma$ of
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}.  The verifier input for a
load-bearing claim $c$ is the following finite record type:
\[
\mathcal C(c)=
\{K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B\}.
\]
Its typed fields are these and only these: $K$ is a finite set of claim kinds;
$\ell\in\{\mathsf{path},\mathsf{command}\}$ is the declared evidence level; $E$
is a finite evidence-surface list; $H$ is the route-boundary field; $R$ is a
finite family of gate pass records, each with gate name, input surface, decision,
evidence pointer, and evidence level; $D$ is either empty or a finite list of
pinned discovery source-interface rows; and $B$ is the command-boundary field.
This is a data schema, not a theorem: all later exactness claims must be proved
from this displayed record and cannot appeal to unlisted package state.  Define
$\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}(c,\mathcal C)$ to be the conjunction of the six finite
table predicates A1--A6 displayed below; no clause may query generated
prose, a live daemon, an artifact evaluator, a proof assistant, or a venue state
outside these fields and their cited submitted surfaces.

\begin{center}
\centering
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{p{0.08\linewidth}p{0.22\linewidth}X}
\toprule
Clause & Field read & Acceptance condition \\
\midrule
A1 & $K,\ell$ & $K$ is a nonempty subset of the seven-kind domain and $\ell$ is one of the two evidence levels. \\
A2 & $E$ & Every evidence item is a submitted path, review-bundle path, manifest row, log path, pinned commit, or explicit historical-evidence boundary available at level $\ell$. \\
A3 & $K,R,E$ & For every gate in $\bigcup_{k\in K}\Gamma(k)$, $R$ has a pass record with gate name, input surface, decision, evidence pointer, and evidence level; the pointer lies in $E$ or in a named submitted table, manifest row, bundled snapshot, or historical boundary. \\
A4 & $H$ & $H$ records human promotion exactly when $c$ crosses the intake-to-publication boundary, and otherwise records that no such crossing occurs. \\
A5 & $K,D$ & $D$ is present exactly when discovery lies in $K$, and then names the pinned discovery-gate source-interface rows used by $c$. \\
A6 & $\ell,B$ & $B$ records command, source commit, environment, exit code, and log path for command-run evidence, or records that no command-run assertion is made. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Finite certificate schema verifier as a record check]
\label{prop:finite-certificate-schema-verifier}
For every load-bearing manuscript claim $c$ whose component kinds lie in the
seven-kind domain, $V(c,\mathcal C)$ is a finite, prose-insensitive
record-schema verifier for the declared publication certificate.  The submitted
package instantiates $V$ by the script
\path{review_bundle/verify_certificate_records.py}.  On the positive package
input it reads the schema file, pass-record ledger, submission-interface map,
primary-claim inventory, and review-bundle manifest named above, and outputs
acceptance in \path{review_bundle/certificate_verification_run.log}.  On the
negative fixture \path{review_bundle/negative_certificate_record_example.json} it
outputs rejection in \path{review_bundle/negative_certificate_record_example_run.md}
with the bad subrecord \path{neg1: command-run fields incomplete}.  If $V$
accepts, then $\mathcal C(c)$ is locally checkable at exactly its declared
evidence level.  This is certificate-record verification only: it checks finite
record shape, dispatch, evidence pointers, and command-boundary discipline under
the audited input/output contract of this paper.  It is not proof-assistant
verification of Python semantics, operating-system behaviour, filesystem
freshness outside the submitted surface, or end-to-end external semantic
validation of the referenced artifacts or source theory.  If $V$ rejects, then a reviewer can extract a finite bad subrecord
consisting of the first failed schema check and the fields on which that check
depends.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The verifier inspects only the displayed tuple $\mathcal C(c)$, the finite
seven-kind domain, the finite dispatch table $\Gamma$, and the finite list of
paths, rows, commits, or logs cited by the record.  The package script realizes
these inputs as five finite JSON files: the schema supplies the seven-kind
domain, evidence levels, gate dispatch table, required record fields, required
pass-record fields, accepted decisions, manifest-required files, and accepted
artifact-prefix patterns; the ledger supplies the seven current records $a_1,
\ldots,a_7$; the submission-interface map and primary-claim inventory supply the
finite manuscript-facing row sets; and the manifest supplies the submitted bundle
paths.  The script output is either the pass transcript in
\path{certificate_verification_run.log} or a list of \path{ERROR: ...} lines,
each naming the failed finite condition.  Since $K$ is required to be a subset of
the seven-kind domain, the set \(\bigcup_{k\in K}\Gamma(k)\) is finite.  The
checks over $E$, $R$, and the command-run fields are therefore finite lookups in
named manuscript or bundle surfaces, not semantic judgments about generated
prose, Python runtime semantics, host-environment correctness, or the truth of
the referenced mathematical or artifact claims.

If all six checks pass, the tuple has exactly the fields required in the
definition of a publication certificate: a finite kind set $K$, declared evidence
level $\ell$, evidence surface $E$, route-boundary field $H$, gate-record field
$R$, optional discovery field $D$ with the required presence condition, and
evidence-strength boundary $B$.  Since $V$ is the conjunction of the explicit
predicates $P_1,\ldots,P_6$, the six table clauses A1--A6 hold for exactly the
same finite inputs.  Check~(ii) is precisely the local-checkability condition on
cited paths, manifest rows, logs, pinned commits, and historical boundaries.
Checks~(iii)--(vi) prevent record-level escalations of the declared level:
missing gate-passage records, unrecorded route promotion, unsupported discovery
routing, and command-run assertion without command-run fields.  Thus an accepted
record is locally checkable at the level $\ell$ it declares, and no stronger
level is silently inferred by the record checker.

If a check fails, the verifier stops at a finite test.  The bad subrecord is the
finite collection of fields read by that failed test: for example, $K$ and
$\Gamma$ for a gate-domain failure, $E$ for an evidence-surface failure, $K$,
$\Gamma$, $R$, and the cited evidence item for a gate-record failure, $H$ for a
promotion failure, $K$ and $D$ for a discovery-field failure, or $\ell$ and $B$
for an evidence-level failure.  The supplied negative fixture is exactly the last
case: it declares $\ell=\mathsf{command}$ but provides no
\path{boundary.command_run_fields} containing command, source commit,
environment, exit code, and log path, so the bad subrecord is the pair consisting
of the evidence-level field and the boundary field.  This subrecord is
independent of any surrounding paragraph that may have described the claim.\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Verifier input--predicate--output contract]
\label{thm:verifier-input-output-contract}
The verifier interface used by the publication-safety theorem is exactly the
following finite mathematical-software contract.  Its input is a pair
$(c,\mathcal C(c))$, where $c$ is a load-bearing manuscript claim and
\(\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)\) is the certificate record of
Definition~\ref{def:certificate-schema-acceptance-table}, together with the fixed
dispatch table $\Gamma$ and the submitted support surface $S$.  Its checked
predicates and outputs are:
\begin{center}
\centering
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{p{0.12\linewidth}p{0.30\linewidth}X}
\toprule
Check & Predicate actually checked & Possible output \\
\midrule
$Q_1$ & $K$ is nonempty, $K\subseteq\mathsf{Dom}(\Gamma)$, and $\ell\in\{\mathsf{path},\mathsf{command}\}$ & accept this coordinate, or reject with bad fields $K,\ell$ \\
$Q_2$ & each item of $E$ is on $S$ or in an explicitly declared pinned, logged, or historical boundary & accept this coordinate, or reject with bad field $E$ and the offending pointer \\
$Q_3$ & every gate assigned by $\Gamma$ to a kind in $K$ has a passing five-field record in $R$ whose pointer is reviewable through $E$, a submitted table, a manifest row, a bundled snapshot, or an historical boundary & accept this coordinate, or reject with bad fields $K,R,E$ and the missing or non-reviewable gate \\
$Q_4$ & $H$ records exactly the human-promotion crossing asserted by $c$, or records that no such crossing is asserted & accept this coordinate, or reject with bad field $H$ \\
$Q_5$ & $D$ is present exactly for discovery-kind claims and then names only pinned source-interface rows used by $c$ & accept this coordinate, or reject with bad fields $K,D$ \\
$Q_6$ & $B$ either contains command, source state, environment, exit code, and log path, or explicitly marks that no command-run assertion is made & accept this coordinate, or reject with bad fields $\ell,B$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
The positive output is only the finite acceptance bit
$\mathsf{accept}(c,\mathcal C)$ for these six predicates.  The negative output is
only the finite bad subrecord belonging to the first failed predicate.  In
particular, the contract has no output channel for proof-assistant validity,
Python or host-environment semantics, daemon correctness, artifact semantics,
fresh case-study reruns, venue upload, or venue acceptance.  Therefore any theorem in this paper that invokes the verifier
can certify exactly finite record acceptance for the submitted schema and cannot
certify end-to-end workflow correctness unless an enlarged input schema and an
additional proved verifier contract are supplied.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The input type is displayed in
Definition~\ref{def:certificate-schema-acceptance-table}: after the fixed table
$\Gamma$ is chosen, the only variable fields are $K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B$.  The
submitted support surface $S$ is used only to decide whether the finite pointers
named in those fields are reviewer-visible at the declared level.  Thus every
listed predicate is a finite Boolean predicate on the displayed input fields and
on the fixed submitted support surface.

For each row, the predicate is identical to one of the six predicates used in the
definition of $V$: $Q_i=P_i$ for $1\leq i\leq 6$, with the same fields read and
with the same failure subrecord, namely the fields read by the least-indexed
failed predicate.  Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-certificate-schema-verifier}
proves that the bundled Python checker is an implementation witness for this
finite schema: it reads the schema, pass-record ledger, submission-interface map,
primary-claim inventory, and manifest, and returns either the pass transcript or
finite error records.  The theorem here is the abstract verifier contract behind
that implementation witness, so its output alphabet is precisely
\(\{\mathsf{accept}\}\) together with the finite bad-subrecord reports.

The final boundary follows by inspection of the input and output alphabets.  No
field in $\mathcal C(c)$ contains an object-language proof derivation, a theorem
prover kernel trace, Python operational semantics, host-environment semantics, a
daemon transition semantics, an artifact evaluator semantics, a fresh rerun
transcript for the historical case studies, or a venue receipt.  No output of the
contract returns such an object either.  A conclusion
depending on one of those objects is therefore not a function of the declared
input record.  It can become checkable only after the schema is enlarged to add
that object as an input coordinate and after a new verifier contract for the
enlarged coordinate is proved.  Hence the present verifier certifies only finite
record acceptance and its finite rejection witnesses.\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Auditable publication-boundary interface completeness]
\label{thm:auditable-compiler-boundary-completeness}
For the architecture of Definition~\ref{def:architecture-axis-map} and the
finite verifier of Theorem~\ref{thm:verifier-input-output-contract}, the software
contribution certified by Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} is
exactly the following publication-boundary interface property.  Every accepted load-bearing
claim in the publication package is the image of a finite input tuple
\[
  (K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B;S,L,\Gamma)
\]
whose evidence fields are on the submitted support surface or in an explicitly
pinned historical boundary, and every rejected stronger reading has a finite bad
subrecord in one of those fields.  Conversely, no fact that is not a function of
this tuple is a publication-boundary output.  In particular, correctness of gate
implementations, Lean/BEDC rebuild success, daemon behaviour, artifact semantic
validity, live case-study reruns, venue upload, archive availability, and venue
acceptance are certified only after the corresponding finite coordinate and
assigned pass record are added to the input tuple.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The displayed architecture table identifies the only publication-boundary input
channels used in this paper: source-interface rows, manifest or witness rows, command-log
rows when present, gate-pass rows, route-promotion rows, and declared limitation
boundaries.  Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface} packages those
channels as \((K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)\) over a submitted support surface \(S\), a
ledger \(L\), and dispatch table \(\Gamma\).  Theorem~\ref{thm:verifier-input-output-contract}
then proves that the verifier reads exactly these fields through the six checks
\(Q_1,\ldots,Q_6\) and has exactly two output types: a finite acceptance bit for
the certificate tuple, or the finite bad subrecord read by the first failed
check.  Therefore every positive finite-record publication-safety conclusion later obtained
from the verifier is an image of the displayed finite tuple, and every negative
conclusion is localized to a finite bad subrecord of that tuple.

It remains to prove exactness of the boundary.  Suppose two surrounding workflow
states agree on \((K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B;S,L,\Gamma)\) but differ in an unread object,
such as the source code of a gate implementation, a proof-assistant checkout, a
daemon trace, an artifact rerun, a venue-upload state, an archive locator, or an
unsubmitted public-source comparison.  The six verifier checks have the same
truth values in the two states, because none of their inputs changed.  Hence a
claim that distinguishes the two states is not determined by the publication
boundary.  This is precisely the finite-coordinate obstruction of
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-coordinate-determination-boundary} and the axis
non-escalation of Proposition~\ref{prop:architecture-axis-non-escalation}.

Conversely, if one of the listed stronger facts is submitted as a finite
coordinate---for example by adding gate source identity, command, source state,
environment, exit code, log path, digest binding, public byte-equality row,
upload-or-archive row, or assigned implementation-gate pass row---then it is no
longer an unread ambient fact.  It is an ordinary extension in the preorder of
Definition~\ref{def:stronger-reading-preorder}.  The finite extension-budget
normal form, Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-extension-budget-normal-form}, says exactly
that the enlarged reading is accepted iff those added coordinates are present and
their assigned gates pass.  Thus the theorem is a completeness statement for the
auditable publication-boundary interface and deliberately not a verified
executable compiler theorem, gate-implementation-correctness theorem, or
semantic-validity theorem outside that boundary.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Support: finite-record verifier normal form]
\label{thm:finite-verifier-normal-form}
Fix the dispatch table $\Gamma$, the submitted support surface $S$, and the
finite certificate schema of Definition~\ref{def:certificate-schema-acceptance-table}.
There is a deterministic verifier
\[
\mathsf{Check}_{\Gamma,S}(c,K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)
\]
with the following presentation-layer input/output normal form.
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{p{0.18\linewidth}p{0.36\linewidth}X}
\toprule
Step & Input fields read & Returned value \\
\midrule
1 & $K,\ell$ & reject with $(Q_1,K,\ell)$, or continue \\
2 & $E$ and $S$ & reject with $(Q_2,E,e_0)$ for the first non-reviewable pointer $e_0$, or continue \\
3 & $K,\Gamma,R,E,S$ & reject with $(Q_3,g,K,R,E)$ for the first missing or non-reviewable assigned gate $g$, or continue \\
4 & $H$ and the route-crossing status of $c$ & reject with $(Q_4,H)$, or continue \\
5 & $K,D$ & reject with $(Q_5,K,D)$, or continue \\
6 & $\ell,B$ & reject with $(Q_6,\ell,B)$, or return $\mathsf{accept}(c,\mathcal C)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
The verifier is an implementation-contract normal form for this finite schema:
as a map from the displayed finite input record to the displayed finite output
alphabet, it is extensionally equal to the predicate $V$ and to the table
relation $\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}$.  It returns acceptance if and only if all six
schema predicates A1--A6 hold, and otherwise returns exactly the first finite
bad subrecord.  This contract is exhausted by the finite record projection: any
script or implementation that claims to witness this theorem witnesses only the
same audited input--predicate--output relation on the submitted fields, not the
correctness of Python semantics, process scheduling, filesystem state outside
\(S\), or the host environment.  In particular,
every positive output used by Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} is
produced by this finite loop over submitted coordinates; the loop has no branch
that can accept a stronger semantic, implementation, venue, archive, or
proof-assistant reading.
The reusable calculus in this paragraph is retained here only as the
schema-relative verifier support needed by the compact spine.  A standalone
software or artifact paper would have to add fresh implementation, environment,
and artifact-semantic coordinates rather than citing this support normal form as
end-to-end verifier correctness.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Define \(\mathsf{Check}_{\Gamma,S}\) by the six displayed steps.  The first step
is predicate $Q_1$, hence predicate $P_1$ and clause A1.  If it fails, the only
fields inspected are $K$ and $\ell$, so the returned subrecord is finite and is
the first possible failed predicate.  If it succeeds, the verifier proceeds to
step~2.  The second step is exactly the evidence-surface predicate $Q_2=P_2$ and
clause A2; since $E$ is a finite list in an accepted certificate candidate and
$S$ is a finite submitted support surface for this package, membership and
boundary tests are finite lookups, and the first offending pointer $e_0$ is a
finite subrecord.  The third step computes the finite assigned-gate set
\(\bigcup_{k\in K}\Gamma(k)\) and applies $Q_3=P_3$, clause A3, to the finite
pass-record list $R$ and the finite reviewable surfaces.  A missing assigned
gate or non-reviewable pass-record pointer therefore yields the displayed finite
subrecord and no semantic countermodel.

The remaining steps are the same identification for the remaining coordinates:
step~4 is $Q_4=P_4$ and A4, step~5 is $Q_5=P_5$ and A5, and step~6 is
$Q_6=P_6$ and A6.  Thus a run reaches the accepting branch exactly when none of
the six schema predicates fails.  This proves extensional equality with
\(V=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{6}P_i\), and Definition~\ref{def:certificate-schema-acceptance-table}
identifies the same conjunction with \(\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}\).  The bad
subrecord is first-failure exact by construction, because the verifier stops at
the least numbered failed step and has inspected only the fields listed in that
row.

Finally, the normal form lists every input coordinate and every output token of
the algorithm.  This is the promised finite-script projection contract: changing
an implementation while preserving the same finite input projection and the same
six comparisons preserves the accepted and rejected output records, and changing
any accepted output requires changing one of the displayed finite predicates or
one of the displayed input fields.  The contract is therefore schema-relative,
not a workflow implementation-soundness assertion.  None of those fields is a proof-assistant
derivation, a theorem-body semantic judgment, an artifact evaluator trace, a
live upload receipt, an archive locator, or a venue decision.  Therefore the
positive branch cannot be read as any of those stronger assertions.  Such an
assertion can be accepted only by enlarging the schema with the missing
coordinate and proving a new input/output contract, as required later by
Theorem~\ref{thm:implementation-soundness-extension-criterion}.\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Schema-relative executable-record acceptance exactness]
\label{thm:record-acceptance-exactness}
Fix the seven-kind dispatch table $\Gamma$, the two evidence levels, and the
typed certificate tuple
$\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)$ of
Definition~\ref{def:certificate-schema-acceptance-table}.  For every
load-bearing claim $c$ and every finite candidate certificate $\mathcal C(c)$,
the finite verifier $V$ of
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:verifier-input-output-contract} accepts $\mathcal C(c)$ if
and only if the six-clause table predicate
$\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}(c,\mathcal C)$ holds.  This is a schema-relative and
finite-record-relative assertion: both sides read exactly the fields named in the
fixed schema and in the finite submitted record surface, and neither side ranges
over unrecorded semantic facts about the referenced mathematics, artifacts, or
gate implementations.  Moreover, if $V$ accepts a record for $c$, the same record
cannot certify any stronger reading $c^{+}$ that adds a new claim kind, a stronger
evidence level, an omitted route crossing, an omitted discovery interface, an
omitted pass record, or a command-run assertion: such a reading has a finite bad
subrecord of the corresponding clause.  Thus $V$ is exact for this paper's finite
record-acceptance relation over the submitted source, tables, manifests, logs,
and explicitly declared historical boundaries, while remaining silent about
external semantic validity of the referenced theory or artifacts and about the
implementation-level soundness of any deployed gate implementation beyond the
recorded pass rows.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The definition of $V$ and the six clauses above use the same finite inputs.
Predicate $P_1$ is clause~A1, $P_2$ is clause~A2, and $P_3$ is clause~A3,
including both assigned-gate coverage and the requirement that each evidence
pointer be tied to the declared review surface.  Predicates $P_4$, $P_5$, and
$P_6$ are exactly clauses~A4, A5, and A6.  Therefore, if
$\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}(c,\mathcal C)$ holds, every verifier predicate is true
and $V$ accepts.

Conversely, suppose $V$ accepts.  Reading the successful checks in order gives
precisely clauses~1--6: the kind set and evidence level are in the permitted
domains; the evidence surface is reviewer-available at the declared level; every
gate assigned by $\Gamma$ has a pass record with the required five fields and an
allowed pointer; promotion and non-promotion are separated by $H$; discovery-kind
claims and only discovery-kind claims carry $D$; and $B$ fixes the command-run
boundary.  Hence $\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}(c,\mathcal C)$ holds.

For the final assertion, keep the accepted tuple fixed and consider a proposed
stronger reading $c^{+}$.  If $c^{+}$ adds a claim kind, the finite set of gates
assigned by $\Gamma$ grows unless the added kind is vacuous in this interface;
without the corresponding pass records clause~3 fails, and if the kind lies
outside the seven-kind domain clause~1 fails.  If $c^{+}$ raises the evidence
level to command-run, clause~6 fails unless the command, commit, environment,
exit code, and log path are present.  If it adds a route crossing, clause~4 fails
unless $H$ contains the human-promotion record.  If it adds discovery content,
clause~5 fails unless the pinned discovery rows are named.  If it asserts a new
gate-dependent conclusion without a pass record, clause~3 fails.  In each case
the failed clause reads only finitely many fields, so deleting irrelevant unread
fields gives an inclusion-minimal bad subrecord.  If none of the clauses changes,
then $c^{+}$ is not stronger in the record semantics: the certificate still
licenses only the same kind set, same evidence level, same gate records, same
route boundary, same discovery interface, and same command boundary.\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Verifier-schema compression of the finite-record calculus]
\label{thm:finite-record-method-schema-compression}
Fix the operational acceptance interface of
Definition~\ref{def:operational-acceptance-interface}, the six-clause acceptance
schema of Definition~\ref{def:certificate-schema-acceptance-table}, and the
finite verifier $V$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-certificate-schema-verifier}.
Let $T$ be any presentation-facing finite-record consequence in this supplement
whose proof uses only the submitted surface $S$, the acceptance ledger $L$, the
dispatch table $\Gamma$, certificate tuples $\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)$,
and first failed schema clauses.  Then $T$ factors through the verifier schema
shown in Figure~\ref{fig:verifier-schema}: its positive part is a statement
about records satisfying $\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}(c,\mathcal C)$, and every
negative or non-escalation part is a statement about the finite bad subrecord
returned by the first failed coordinate among $K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B$.  Consequently
the compact CICM presentation may replace the repetitive finite-record lemmas by
the single method interface consisting of
Theorems~\ref{thm:record-acceptance-exactness} and
\ref{thm:finite-record-method-schema-compression} together with
Figure~\ref{fig:verifier-schema}, without changing any accepted certificate or
any rejected stronger reading.  The compression is exact only at the declared
record level: it does not add implementation soundness, proof-assistant rebuild
truth, artifact semantics, fresh command execution, upload/archive status, or
venue acceptance.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The hypotheses defining $T$ mention no object except $S$, $L$, $\Gamma$, the
seven certificate fields, and the first failed schema clause.  By
Theorem~\ref{thm:record-acceptance-exactness}, the predicate computed by $V$ is
extensionally equal, on exactly those finite inputs, to the six-clause relation
$\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}(c,\mathcal C)$.  Hence every positive occurrence of
``accepted'', ``covered by assigned gates'', ``path-verified at level $\ell$'',
``human-promoted'', ``discovery-interface supplied'', or ``command-run boundary
satisfied'' in such a consequence can be rewritten as the corresponding schema
coordinate in Figure~\ref{fig:verifier-schema}.  This gives the stated
factorisation for the positive part.

For a negative or sharpness assertion, the same exactness theorem says that a
properly stronger reading changes at least one finite coordinate: it adds a claim
kind, raises the evidence level, changes the evidence surface, requires an
additional pass row, adds promotion or discovery content, or asserts command-run
strength.  The verifier checks these coordinates in the six schema clauses; if
the required coordinate is absent, the first failed clause reads finitely many
fields and returns the bad subrecord used by the consequence.  Removing fields
not read by that failed clause preserves failure, so the rejection depends only
on the displayed bad-coordinate row of Figure~\ref{fig:verifier-schema}.

Thus replacing the individual finite-record consequences by the schema theorem
and figure preserves exactly the accepted records and exactly the rejected
stronger readings.  Since the schema reads no source code semantics, Lean build
state, artifact evaluator semantics, external upload state, archive locator, or
venue decision, no compressed statement can acquire any of those stronger
meanings.  The result is therefore a reusable software-schema theorem for the
presentation paper, while the remaining record lemmas in this supplement are its
finite pullback instances.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Executable schema exactness and negative fixture]
\label{cor:executable-schema-exactness-negative-fixture}
Under the hypotheses and fixed schema of
Theorem~\ref{thm:record-acceptance-exactness}, the executable verifier instance
\path{review_bundle/verify_certificate_records.py} is a finite witness of the
same schema-relative relation, not an additional semantic oracle.  On the positive
submitted package it can witness exactly the records satisfying
\(\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}\) at their declared evidence levels.  On the negative
fixture
\path{review_bundle/negative_certificate_record_example.json}, which upgrades a
route record to command-run strength while omitting the command, source state,
environment, exit code, and log path, the extracted bad subrecord is exactly the
evidence-level declaration together with the incomplete boundary field.  Hence
the executable example separates the verifier contract from any stronger reading:
changing prose or ambient pipeline state while keeping the finite schema fields
fixed cannot change either the acceptance bit or the first failed finite
subrecord.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-certificate-schema-verifier} identifies the script
\path{review_bundle/verify_certificate_records.py}, the schema files it reads,
and the two recorded runs.  Its positive run returns the finite acceptance
transcript for the submitted records, and its negative run returns the reported
finite error \path{neg1: command-run fields incomplete}.  By
Theorem~\ref{thm:verifier-input-output-contract}, those are the only two output
kinds of the verifier contract: acceptance of the six predicates or a bad
subrecord for the first failed predicate.  By
Theorem~\ref{thm:record-acceptance-exactness}, positive acceptance is equivalent
to \(\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}\) for the same tuple
\((K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)\).  In the negative fixture, clauses A1--A4 and the
non-discovery discipline are supplied for the route row, while the declared
command-run level triggers clause A6 and the required five command-run fields are
absent.  The first failed predicate therefore reads exactly \(\ell\) and \(B\),
so deleting any unrelated prose, score, route history, or ambient implementation
state leaves the same failure.  The script is thus an executable finite-record
witness for the schema-relative theorem and for its negative certificate example,
not evidence of an unrecorded semantic rerun or gate-implementation proof.\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-coordinate determination and trust-boundary classifier]
\label{thm:finite-coordinate-determination-boundary}
Fix the dispatch table $\Gamma$ and the verifier $V$.  Let $F_{\Gamma}$ be the
finite schema projection read by $V$ from a certificate record, namely the
claim-kind set, declared evidence level, evidence surface, promotion field,
gate-pass rows, discovery-source rows, command-boundary tuple, and the assigned
gate set determined by $\Gamma$.  If two ambient pipeline or artifact states
induce the same values of all coordinates in $F_{\Gamma}$ for a claim $c$, then
they induce the same record-acceptance decision and the same finite publication
certificate for $c$.  Therefore the exactness of
Theorem~\ref{thm:record-acceptance-exactness} is exactness only relative to this
finite schema projection.  No property depending on a coordinate outside
$F_{\Gamma}$---for example the semantic truth of a referenced theorem, truthful
production or implementation soundness of a gate row, a fresh Lean build result,
a daemon trace, an artifact semantic fact, a theorem-environment completeness
claim, or an external venue decision---is a consequence of the accepted
certificate unless that property is first encoded as an additional finite
certificate coordinate and the enlarged record is accepted.  In particular,
record-gate soundness is a load-bearing hypothesis for
Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface}; it is not supplied by schema
exactness alone.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The verifier $V$ is defined as an ordered list of six checks, and each check reads
only one of the coordinates listed in $F_{\Gamma}$ together with the fixed finite
dispatch table $\Gamma$.  If two ambient states induce the same values on
$F_{\Gamma}$, then the input tuple \((K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)\), the assigned gate set,
and every submitted pointer queried by $V$ are identical in the two states.  Each
of the six checks therefore has the same truth value in the two states, so $V$
either accepts both records or rejects both records at the same first failed
finite field.  By Theorem~\ref{thm:record-acceptance-exactness}, an accepted
decision is equivalent to the same six-clause record-acceptance semantics, hence
the finite certificate determined by those clauses is also the same.  This proves
the schema-relative and finite-record-relative factorisation.

Now let $Q$ be a property whose truth can vary while all coordinates in
$F_{\Gamma}$ are held fixed.  Then there exist two ambient states with the same
certificate tuple and the same verifier decision but different truth values for
$Q$.  A conclusion whose truth changes under such an $F_{\Gamma}$-preserving
substitution is not determined by the accepted certificate.  To make $Q$
load-bearing, the operational interface must add a finite coordinate recording
the required evidence: for a build or daemon trace this is a command-run tuple;
for an artifact semantic fact this is an artifact pass record or fresh evaluator
rerun log; for theorem-environment completeness this is an extractor command,
source state, environment, exit code, and log path; and for a venue decision this
is an external evidence surface and the corresponding route/submission record.
Without that enlargement, Theorem~\ref{thm:record-acceptance-exactness} supplies
only the original finite-record conclusion.

Finally, the same argument isolates record-gate soundness.  The predicate
$\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)$ says that recorded ledger entries actually contain
the assigned passing rows and submitted evidence pointers.  A package can agree
on the schema shape of a candidate certificate while differing on whether such a
record-gate-sound ledger has been supplied.  Thus schema exactness checks the
finite acceptance relation after the row data are present; it does not by itself
make those rows available, truthfully produced, or semantically adequate.
Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} therefore states record-gate
soundness as an explicit hypothesis, and the trust boundary is exactly the finite
projection $F_{\Gamma}$ plus that hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Record-interface rigidity and refresh fixed point]
\label{thm:record-interface-rigidity}
Fix a package $P$, submitted support surface $S$, finite ledger $L$, dispatch
table $\Gamma$, and certificate tuple
$\mathcal C(c)=(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)$ for each accepted load-bearing claim
$c\in L$.  Let $\pi_{\Gamma,S}(P,L)$ be the finite projection consisting of the
tuple fields $(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)$, the gate-pass rows in $R$, the submitted
support-surface membership relation for $S$, and the fixed dispatch table
$\Gamma$.  Then the following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The ledger satisfies the external record-gate interface
\(\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)\) and the verifier accepts every displayed
certificate.
\item The finite projection $\pi_{\Gamma,S}(P,L)$ is a fixed point of the six
schema checks: re-reading the projected rows, evidence pointers, gate assignments,
promotion field, discovery field, and command-boundary field reconstructs the
same family of certificates and produces no new accepted coordinate.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover this fixed point is rigid.  Any proper stronger reading of an accepted
claim---including gate-implementation soundness, fresh command rerun success,
artifact-semantic validity, semantic theorem-inventory completeness, upload
status, or venue acceptance---is accepted by the same interface if and only if it
adds a nonempty finite extension coordinate to
$(K,\ell,E,H,R,D,B)$ or to $R$ and the enlarged projection again satisfies the
fixed-point condition.  In particular, after a submitted support file used by the
projection is regenerated, the current-package finite-record claim is restored
only by the finite refresh sequence that regenerates the dependent theorem
environment inventory, certificate-verifier log, source-interface-verifier log,
primary-claim verifier log, and final digest surface so that all paths and digest
rows are again read from one common projection.  Without that common projection,
the TeX theorem chain retains only its source-level statements and not a
machine-readable current-package exactness claim.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Assume first that \(\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)\) holds and that every displayed
certificate is accepted.  By
Proposition~\ref{prop:record-gate-soundness-external-interface-exactness}, the
interface supplies exactly the certificates whose evidence surfaces lie in $S$,
whose assigned gate rows are present and passing, whose evidence pointers denote
submitted elements at the recorded evidence level, and whose promotion,
discovery, and command-boundary fields satisfy the verifier predicates.  Applying
Theorem~\ref{thm:record-acceptance-exactness} to each row identifies this with
the six-clause relation $\mathsf{Acc}_{\Gamma}$.  Hence re-reading precisely the
fields in $\pi_{\Gamma,S}(P,L)$ repeats the same six checks and returns the same
certificate family; no seventh field or stronger coordinate is read by any check.
This is the stated fixed point.

Conversely suppose the finite projection is such a fixed point.  The fixed-point
condition states, field by field, that the kind and evidence-level fields pass
the domain check, that every evidence pointer lies on $S$, that every assigned
gate in $\bigcup_{k\in K}\Gamma(k)$ has a passing row in $R$, that the promotion
coordinate is present exactly when required, and that the discovery and
command-boundary coordinates satisfy the presence conditions of $P_5$ and $P_6$.
These are exactly the positive-output clauses of
Definition~\ref{def:record-gate-soundness-external-interface}.  Therefore
\(\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)\) holds, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:record-acceptance-exactness} gives verifier acceptance for the
same displayed certificates.

It remains to prove rigidity.  Let $c^{+}$ be a proper stronger reading of an
accepted claim.  By Definition~\ref{def:stronger-reading-preorder}, being proper
means that at least one of the finite coordinates $K$, $\ell$, $E$, $H$, $R$,
$D$, or $B$ is strictly enlarged.  If the enlarged tuple and any added pass rows
again satisfy the six schema checks, the preceding equivalence applied to the
enlarged projection accepts $c^{+}$.  Conversely, if $c^{+}$ is accepted by the
same finite interface, Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-coordinate-determination-boundary}
forces the acceptance decision to be determined by a finite coordinate read by
the verifier.  Since $c^{+}$ is not record-equivalent to $c$, at least one such
coordinate is new or strictly enlarged; otherwise the two readings would have the
same projection and hence the same bounded certificate meaning.  Thus every
proper stronger reading has positive finite extension budget and no stronger
reading is obtained for free from the original fixed point.

The listed examples are exactly instances of this coordinate test.  Gate
implementation soundness requires implementation source, specification,
environment, command or implementation-gate records, and logs.  Fresh rerun
success requires command, source state, environment, exit code, and log path.
Artifact-semantic validity requires an artifact-semantic evidence surface or
evaluator pass row.  Semantic theorem-inventory completeness requires an
extractor command, source-to-inventory binding, produced inventory, and pass row.
Upload and venue readings require external route, submission, or decision
records.  None is among the old projection unless it is explicitly added.

Finally suppose a file on the submitted support surface is regenerated.  The
membership and digest facts read by $P_2$, the pass-row facts read by $P_3$, and
the command-boundary facts read by $P_6$ then refer to a changed byte coordinate.
The fixed-point implication can be applied again only after the finite surfaces
that mirror that coordinate have been recomputed from the same bytes: the theorem
environment extractor supplies the theorem-inventory coordinate, the certificate
verifier supplies the schema-acceptance coordinate, the source-interface verifier
supplies the imported-source coordinate, the primary-claim verifier supplies the
retained-claim coordinate, and the final digest surface supplies the byte identity
shared by the submitted support relation.  If one of these surfaces is stale, two
ambient states can agree on the printed TeX prose while disagreeing on a byte
coordinate read by the projection, so the machine-readable current-package
exactness conclusion is not determined.  What remains is only the TeX-level
statement already proved independently of that regenerated support surface.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Record-gate implementation overclaim obstruction]
\label{thm:record-gate-implementation-overclaim-obstruction}
The hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} and the fixed
point of Theorem~\ref{thm:record-interface-rigidity} determine finite certificate
construction under the external record-gate interface
\(\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)\), but they do not determine correctness of any
gate implementation that produced, stored, or displayed the pass rows.  More
precisely, for any accepted claim row $c$, a finite-record
implementation-soundness reading for the gates assigned to $c$ is accepted by the
same calculus if and only if both of the following positive coordinates are added
to the support surface.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The package support surface contains a nonempty implementation coordinate
for those gates: gate source identity, source digest or commit, command line,
runtime environment, input records, output records, exit code, log path, digest
binding to the submitted support surface, negative-fixture or regression rows
where the gate contract uses them, and an assigned implementation-gate pass row.
\item The package states an independent implementation-soundness contract for
that coordinate: the contract names the intended specification, the checked source
state, the test or proof obligation family, the produced logs, and the finite
criterion by which those logs imply the implementation-soundness predicate being
claimed.
\end{enumerate}
Without this coordinate, every implementation-soundness reading has a finite bad
subrecord, while the bounded certificate-construction reading remains valid under
record-gate soundness.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:publication-safety-interface} uses
\(\mathsf{RGS}_{S}(P,L,\Gamma)\) as an external hypothesis: the required finite
pass rows and evidence pointers are present on the submitted surface.  It then
